history.meaning: Animal and food exposures bring brucellosis, Q fever, leptospirosis, and toxoplasmosis into the differential. These are serologic diagnoses — you only find them if the exposure history prompts the right tests.

history.question: Have you started any new medications or supplements recently, or do you have any implanted medical devices?
listenFor: No new medications or implanted devices
New medication without known drug fever risk
New drug fever risk medication or implanted device/line
history.meaning: Drug fever is a diagnosis of exclusion that resolves when the drug stops, and devices harbor indolent infection. This history suggests a trial of stopping the suspect drug and examining every device — a reversible cause hiding in plain sight.

history.question: Do you have a history of cancer, autoimmune disease, or any condition that suppresses your immune system?
listenFor: No history of immunosuppression or malignancy
Active hematologic malignancy, chemotherapy, or severe immunosuppression
history.meaning: A history of malignancy or autoimmunity puts lymphoma, recurrence, and opportunistic infection at the top. It frames the whole workup — imaging for recurrence, broader infectious testing — and lowers the threshold for tissue diagnosis.

exam.maneuver: Assess body temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, and overall clinical appearance.
exam.meaning: Documenting the fever pattern and looking sick versus well sets the urgency. A toxic patient needs admission and an expedited workup; a well patient with prolonged fever can be worked up methodically as an outpatient.

exam.maneuver: Inspect skin, mucosal surfaces, and conjunctivae for rashes, petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, or jaundice.
findings: Skin intact, no rash or lesions
Petechiae, purpura, splinter hemorrhages, or jaundice
exam.meaning: Rashes, petechiae, splinter hemorrhages, and jaundice are visible clues to vasculitis, endocarditis, or liver disease. Finding one can shortcut weeks of testing — biopsy the lesion or follow the clue.

exam.maneuver: Palpate cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes.
exam.meaning: Generalized adenopathy suggests lymphoma, TB, or HIV; isolated supraclavicular nodes raise malignancy. The pattern decides between excisional biopsy, infectious testing, or oncology referral.

exam.maneuver: Auscultate the heart for murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
findings: New diastolic or changing murmur, or pericardial rub
exam.meaning: A new murmur raises endocarditis; a rub suggests pericarditis. These findings redirect the workup to echocardiography and blood cultures.

exam.maneuver: Auscultate lungs for crackles, wheezing, or decreased breath sounds.
findings: Diffuse crackles, rub, or absent breath sounds
exam.meaning: Focal findings point to TB, pneumonia, or pulmonary infarction; clear lungs push the search elsewhere. The exam decides whether chest imaging leads the workup.

exam.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for tenderness, masses, or organomegaly (hepatosplenomegaly).
findings: Focal tenderness, guarding, palpable mass, or hepatosplenomegaly
exam.meaning: Hepatosplenomegaly suggests lymphoma, EBV, or disseminated infection; a mass suggests malignancy or abscess. These findings direct imaging to the abdomen and often to tissue diagnosis.

exam.maneuver: Percuss the costovertebral angles for tenderness.
exam.meaning: Flank tenderness points to a renal source — pyelonephritis, renal abscess, or infected stones. It adds renal imaging and urine cultures to the FUO workup.

exam.maneuver: Examine joints for swelling, erythema, warmth, or tenderness, and inspect temporal arteries.
findings: No joint swelling or temporal artery tenderness
Active synovitis, joint effusion, or tender/thickened temporal arteries
exam.meaning: Swollen joints suggest Still disease or vasculitis; tender temporal arteries in an older adult mean giant cell arteritis. The latter is an emergency — start steroids immediately to prevent blindness and arrange temporal artery biopsy.

exam.maneuver: Assess neck mobility for rigidity or signs of meningismus.
findings: Supple neck, full range of motion
Nuchal rigidity, positive Brudzinski or Kernig signs
exam.meaning: Nuchal rigidity with prolonged fever raises chronic meningitis — TB or fungal. This finding means lumbar puncture with opening pressure and specific testing, not just routine studies.

exam.maneuver: Inspect the dentition, pharynx, and sinuses.
findings: Dental abscess, dental caries, or tonsillar exudates
exam.meaning: Dental abscesses and sinusitis are classic occult sources of prolonged fever. Finding one gives you a treatable source — a dental referral or sinus imaging — that a broad workup might miss.

history.question: Have you had persistent fevers, night sweats, fatigue, or unexplained weight loss?
listenFor: High fevers, night sweats, and weight loss
history.meaning: This constitutional pattern is the classic subacute presentation — weeks of low-grade bacteremia rather than an abrupt sepsis. It includes endocarditis in a patient whose fever has no clear source and means drawing blood cultures before any antibiotics, drawn properly.

history.question: Do you have a history of valve disease, a heart murmur, a prosthetic valve, or a cardiac device?
listenFor: No history of valve disease or cardiac device
Known heart murmur or valve disease
Prosthetic heart valve or implanted cardiac device
history.meaning: Damaged or prosthetic valves and cardiac devices are where vegetations form — this is the single biggest risk factor. A yes dramatically raises pretest probability, so even vague symptoms trigger blood cultures and an echocardiogram.

history.question: Have you used intravenous drugs, or have you had recent dental work or surgeries?
listenFor: No IV drug use or recent invasive procedures
Recent minor surgery or dental cleaning
Active intravenous drug use or major dental surgery/extraction
history.meaning: IV drug use seeds right-sided valves; dental procedures cause transient bacteremia that seeds damaged valves. This history identifies the at-risk patient and the likely organisms — staph for IV drug use — guiding empiric coverage.

history.question: Have you had new shortness of breath, chest pain, or swelling in your legs?
listenFor: Mild exertional dyspnea or trace leg edema
Orthopnea, chest pain, or severe peripheral edema
history.meaning: New heart failure symptoms mean the valve is failing — regurgitation from a destroyed valve. This includes hemodynamically significant endocarditis and means an urgent echo plus cardiology and cardiac surgery consults, because a failing valve needs an operation.

history.question: Have you noticed any new painful or painless spots, bumps, or lines on your skin, fingers, or toes?
listenFor: Splinter hemorrhages, painful nodules on fingers, or painless red spots on palms/soles
history.meaning: Osler nodes (painful) and Janeway lesions (painless) plus splinter hemorrhages are the immunologic and embolic stigmata of endocarditis. They strongly support the diagnosis clinically and push toward blood cultures and echo without delay.

history.question: Have you had a sudden weakness, numbness, vision changes, or severe headache?
listenFor: Acute focal weakness, sensory loss, vision changes, or meningeal headache
history.meaning: Septic emboli to the brain cause stroke, and mycotic aneurysms can rupture — the neurologic complications of endocarditis. A yes means a head CT, neurology input, and caution with anticoagulation, since hemorrhagic conversion is a real risk.

history.question: Have you noticed blood in your urine or flank pain?
listenFor: Gross hematuria or acute flank pain
history.meaning: Blood in the urine with flank pain suggests renal emboli or immune-complex glomerulonephritis from endocarditis. It includes embolic kidney injury and means checking kidney function and urinalysis as part of the embolic workup.

history.question: Have you had new joint pain or back pain?
listenFor: Severe localized back pain or acute joint swelling
history.meaning: Septic emboli can seed joints and the spine — septic arthritis or vertebral osteomyelitis as complications. New musculoskeletal pain in this context needs imaging and possibly aspiration, not just pain control.

history.question: Have you taken antibiotics recently before your blood cultures were drawn?
listenFor: Completed antibiotic course over 2 weeks ago
Recent or active antibiotic use within past 2 weeks
history.meaning: Prior antibiotics sterilize blood cultures and are the main reason endocarditis goes undiagnosed. Knowing this means holding further antibiotics until cultures are drawn and warning the lab, since partially treated endocarditis needs a longer course.

history.question: Do you have an indwelling venous line, hemodialysis catheter, or a history of recurrent bloodstream infections?
listenFor: No indwelling catheters or recurrent infections
Active central line, hemodialysis catheter, or prior bacteremia
history.meaning: Lines and dialysis catheters are the source of repeated bacteremia that seeds valves. This history means the line likely needs to come out, cultures come from the line and the periphery, and the echo threshold stays low.

exam.maneuver: Auscultate the heart for a new murmur or changes to an existing murmur.
findings: No murmur or stable chronic murmur
New diastolic murmur or changing murmur severity
exam.meaning: A new regurgitant murmur is the cardinal physical sign of valvular endocarditis. It cements the diagnosis clinically and means urgent echocardiography plus cardiology and cardiac surgery involvement for possible valve intervention.

exam.maneuver: Assess body temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, and perfusion status.
exam.meaning: Fever with tachycardia confirms active infection; hypotension or poor perfusion warns of sepsis or acute valve failure. The exam sets the tempo — unstable means ICU, pressors, and emergent surgical evaluation.

exam.maneuver: Inspect palms and soles for painless, erythematous macular lesions (Janeway lesions).
exam.meaning: Painless erythematous macules on the palms and soles are septic emboli — they clinch the clinical picture of endocarditis. Finding them strengthens the diagnosis and prompts a search for other embolic sites.

exam.maneuver: Inspect pads of fingers and toes for painful, erythematous nodules (Osler nodes).
exam.meaning: Painful nodules on the finger and toe pads are the immunologic stigmata of endocarditis. They support the diagnosis and, like Janeway lesions, mean the full endocarditis workup proceeds without delay.

exam.maneuver: Inspect fingernails and toenails for linear dark red streaks (splinter hemorrhages).
exam.meaning: Linear red streaks under the nails are another embolic and immunologic sign. Alone they are nonspecific, but in a febrile patient with a murmur they add weight to endocarditis and support moving to echo.

exam.maneuver: Examine the conjunctivae for petechiae and perform fundoscopy to assess for retinal hemorrhages (Roth spots) if trained.
findings: Roth spots present on fundoscopic exam
exam.meaning: Petechiae and retinal hemorrhages with white centers are the eye's report of embolic and immunologic phenomena. Finding them supports the diagnosis and means ophthalmology documents the extent of embolic disease.

exam.maneuver: Auscultate lungs for crackles, wheezing, or evidence of pulmonary congestion.
findings: Diffuse bilateral crackles indicating heart failure
exam.meaning: Crackles suggest heart failure from valve destruction; in IV drug use with tricuspid endocarditis, septic pulmonary emboli cause the lung findings. The exam distinguishes left-sided valve failure from right-sided septic emboli, changing the surgical conversation.

exam.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for splenomegaly or left upper quadrant tenderness.
findings: No splenomegaly or left upper quadrant tenderness
Left upper quadrant tenderness without splenomegaly
Palpable splenomegaly or severe tender splenic infarct findings
exam.meaning: An enlarged tender spleen reflects immune activation and possible splenic emboli or abscess. It supports the diagnosis and means watching for splenic rupture or abscess — a surgical concern.

exam.maneuver: Perform a focused neurologic exam assessing strength, sensation, cranial nerves, and signs of embolic stroke.
findings: New focal neurologic deficit (hemiparesis, aphasia) suggesting embolic event
exam.meaning: A focal deficit means a septic cerebral embolus — stroke from the vegetation. This finding means a head CT, a neurology consult, and rethinking anticoagulation and surgical timing, since brain hemorrhage changes everything.

exam.maneuver: Inspect any indwelling catheter or line site for erythema, warmth, tenderness, or purulent drainage.
findings: No indwelling lines, or line site is clean and quiet
Mild erythema without drainage at line site
Erythema, purulent drainage, or tenderness at line site
exam.meaning: An inflamed line site identifies the source of the bacteremia seeding the valve. It means removing the line, culturing it, and treating the bloodstream infection at its origin.

history.question: What brought you in today? What is most important to address?
listenFor: Chief concern in patient's own words
history.meaning: Start with her own words before the chart anchors you. On a busy triage unit the chart tells one story and she'll tell you another, and the complaint she names first sets your triage sequence: pain plus bleeding gets the placenta workup first, headache plus vision changes gets the preeclampsia workup first. Her answer also tells you what she fears most, which is what you need to address before she can hear anything else. If her priority doesn't match the chart, believe her and re-triage.

history.question: Could you be pregnant? Are you trying to conceive?
history.meaning: Pregnancy rewrites the entire differential, so you establish it before any test, drug, or image. Abdominal pain with a positive test is ectopic until proven otherwise, and every medication choice and imaging decision changes the moment pregnancy is on the table. If she could be pregnant, get a urine hCG on every patient with pelvic pain or vaginal bleeding, hold teratogenic meds, and shield the abdomen from unnecessary radiation. If she's trying to conceive, counsel on preconception folic acid and early prenatal care, and keep ectopic and miscarriage in the differential for any first-trimester complaint.

history.question: When was the first day of your last normal period (LMP)?
history.meaning: The last menstrual period anchors gestational dating, and dating drives every decision on L&D: whether contractions are preterm labor or term labor, whether she's post-term, and how you counsel about viability. A vague or unreliable LMP is itself information, because acting on a wrong date means delivering too early or letting a post-term pregnancy go too long. If the LMP is reliable and matches her size, use it; if it's unreliable, unknown, or discordant with the exam, get the earliest ultrasound available to redate before you make any delivery-versus-wait decision.

history.question: Have you had a home or clinic pregnancy test?
history.meaning: History alone never rules out pregnancy, and you don't want to discover it after the CT or the prescription. A positive test with pain or bleeding triggers the ectopic workup immediately, while a negative test redirects you to non-pregnant causes like appendicitis, ovarian torsion, or UTI. If the test is positive with pelvic pain or bleeding, order a quantitative hCG and a pelvic ultrasound to confirm the pregnancy is intrauterine. If she hasn't tested at all, get one stat in triage before anything else happens.

history.question: What is your gestational age and estimated due date (EDD), and how was the pregnancy dated?
history.meaning: Gestational age is the single most management-defining number in obstetrics. It tells you whether contractions are preterm (steroids, GBS prophylaxis, and magnesium for neuroprotection enter the picture) or term (delivery is fine), and whether she's post-term (induction is warranted). How the pregnancy was dated tells you how much to trust the number: first-trimester ultrasound dating is the gold standard, while LMP dating in an irregular cycler is suspect. If dates are uncertain, confirm them before deciding to deliver or to wait, because the EDD sets the timing of every intervention from amniocentesis to induction.

history.question: Have you had prenatal care this pregnancy?
history.meaning: No prenatal care means a blank slate at the highest triage risk tier: unknown gestation, unknown GBS status, unscreened HIV, syphilis, and hepatitis B, unknown anatomy, and unknown complications. It also tells you the records you were hoping for don't exist. Lower your threshold for the full workup: stat infectious labs, a bedside ultrasound for dating and fetal number, blood pressure and urine protein, and assume unknown GBS so she gets penicillin in labor. These patients get observed, not fast-discharged.

history.question: Is this one baby or more than one (fetal number)?
history.meaning: Twins multiply the stakes: higher risk of preterm labor, preeclampsia, malpresentation, cord prolapse, and postpartum hemorrhage from an overdistended uterus. A patient who thinks she's carrying a singleton but has an undiagnosed twin is a setup for catastrophe, and fundal height bigger than dates is the classic clue. If fetal number is unknown or discordant, confirm it on ultrasound now. Multiples change delivery planning (position of twin B, anesthesia, NICU availability) and lower your threshold for admitting preterm contractions.

history.question: Any complications or medications in this pregnancy?
history.meaning: The complication list tells you what's already going wrong and the medication list tells you what's controlling it, or what's dangerous. Anticoagulants change your anesthesia options and hemorrhage risk, antihypertensives have pregnancy-safe and unsafe choices, and some drugs are outright teratogenic. Reconcile every drug for pregnancy safety and labor implications before you prescribe anything new. Use the list to generate the surveillance plan: headache in a patient with known chronic hypertension moves superimposed preeclampsia to the top, and bleeding on anticoagulation has an iatrogenic contributor you need to account for.

history.question: Are you having any vaginal bleeding?
history.meaning: Bleeding in pregnancy is never normal and always gets worked up. The character narrows it fast: painless bright-red bleeding late in pregnancy is placenta previa until proven otherwise, while painful dark bleeding with a uterus that won't relax is abruption. Other can't-miss causes include vasa previa (bleeding with membrane rupture plus fetal heart rate decelerations, an emergency), preterm labor with bloody show, and miscarriage by trimester. Any bleeding in the second half means no digital exam until previa is excluded on ultrasound; do a speculum exam instead. Heavy bleeding or abruption signs mean type and cross, large-bore IVs, continuous monitoring, and preparation for emergent delivery.

history.question: Are you having contractions?
history.meaning: The contraction pattern is what separates true labor from Braxton Hicks: true labor is regular, painful, and builds in frequency, duration, and intensity with cervical change, while Braxton Hicks are irregular and ease with rest or hydration. Pin down onset, frequency, and duration up front so you know how far along the process is. Regular painful contractions with cervical change at term mean admit for labor; irregular contractions with a closed cervix mean hydrate, observe, and discharge with return precautions. Preterm regular contractions trigger the preterm labor workup with steroids, GBS prophylaxis, and transfer considerations, while painful frequent contractions with a uterus that never relaxes point to abruption and continuous monitoring.

history.question: Any leakage of fluid?
listenFor: Possible fluid leakage / rupture of membranes
history.meaning: A gush or steady leak usually means ruptured membranes, and from that moment the clock starts on ascending infection: longer latency means higher chorioamnionitis risk. Preterm rupture is one of the most management-intensive diagnoses in obstetrics. Confirm it on speculum exam with pooling, ferning, and nitrazine, and never do a digital exam, which seeds infection upward. Confirmed preterm rupture means admit, antenatal steroids, latency antibiotics, GBS prophylaxis, and magnesium for neuroprotection under 32 weeks; confirmed term rupture means plan delivery rather than prolonged waiting. Fever or uterine tenderness after rupture means suspected chorioamnionitis: broad-spectrum antibiotics and move to delivery.

history.question: How has the baby's movement been?
history.meaning: Maternal perception of decreased fetal movement is one of the most reliable early warnings of fetal compromise: the fetus conserves energy and moves less when placental function fails, often before the heart tracing looks bad. This question catches stillbirth risk while there's still time to act. Never reassure decreased movement over the phone; bring her in for a nonstress test and biophysical profile, and look for abruption or preeclampsia as the cause. Reassuring testing means kick-count counseling and strict return precautions, while non-reassuring testing means delivery planning with urgency driven by gestational age and the tracing.

history.question: Any severe headache, vision change, right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain, marked swelling, fever, burning with urination, or trauma?
history.meaning: This is the red-flag bundle that catches the two big killers on L&D. Severe headache, vision changes, right-upper-quadrant or epigastric pain, and sudden marked swelling point to preeclampsia with severe features, where RUQ pain means liver capsule stretch until proven otherwise. Fever, dysuria, or uterine tenderness point to intrauterine infection, and trauma raises abruption. Headache, vision changes, or RUQ pain mean stat blood pressure, urine protein, and labs with CBC, liver enzymes, and creatinine, plus magnesium for seizure prophylaxis and delivery planning if preeclampsia with severe features is confirmed. Fever means evaluate for chorioamnionitis and start broad-spectrum antibiotics with delivery planning, and trauma means Kleihauer-Betke testing, Rhogam if she's Rh-negative, and monitoring for abruption.

history.question: How old were you when your periods started (menarche)?
history.meaning: Menarche age sets the reproductive timeline, and very early or very late menarche signals an endocrine disorder that may still be driving today's complaint. Late menarche points toward primary ovarian insufficiency, Turner syndrome, hypothalamic amenorrhea from undernutrition or heavy exercise, or an outflow obstruction; early menarche suggests precocious puberty and a possible PCOS trajectory. Late menarche with current irregular bleeding earns an FSH and AMH check and a POI workup with bone and cardiac counseling plus a hormone replacement discussion. Early menarche is mostly historical context, but it flags a longer lifetime estrogen exposure relevant to breast and endometrial risk counseling.

history.question: Are your periods regular — every how many days, bleeding for how many days?
history.meaning: Regularity is the best bedside test for ovulation: regular cycles almost always mean she's ovulating, so the bleeding problem is structural or a bleeding disorder, while irregular cycles mean anovulation until proven otherwise. This one question prunes the workup dramatically. Regular heavy bleeding points to fibroids, adenomyosis, or a coagulopathy, especially von Willebrand disease if it's been heavy since menarche. Irregular bleeding points to PCOS, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, or perimenopause, so check TSH, prolactin, and androgens and treat the cause rather than just suppressing the bleeding.

history.question: Has there been a recent change in your periods?
history.meaning: A new change in a previously stable pattern is the red flag that separates chronic benign bleeding from new pathology; cycles don't suddenly change without a reason. New irregularity in a perimenopausal patient or new heavy bleeding at any age earns a real workup, not reassurance. The differential for new change is pregnancy, new fibroid or polyp growth, endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, new medications like anticoagulants, and thyroid disease. Start with a pregnancy test, then evaluate structurally with ultrasound and sample the endometrium if age or risk factors warrant; don't just prescribe hormones to mask a change you haven't explained.

history.question: How heavy is your flow — pads, tampons, or cup per day? Do you fully soak them?
listenFor: Pads / tampons / cup per day, not soaked
history.meaning: Heavy is subjective, so pads or tampons per day and whether they soak through define heavy menstrual bleeding in a way you can act on and track over time. Quantifying flow also screens for anemia before labs come back: soaking through hourly or passing large clots with dizziness is urgent. Heavy bleeding since menarche points to von Willebrand disease or another coagulopathy, while new heavy flow points to fibroids, adenomyosis, polyps, or anovulatory cycles. Check hemoglobin and ferritin, treat iron deficiency, and use the baseline number as your yardstick for whether treatment with tranexamic acid, a hormonal IUD, or a procedure is actually working.

history.question: How do your periods affect your life?
history.meaning: This is the question that decides whether treatment is indicated, because abnormal uterine bleeding gets treated when it bothers the patient, not when a lab value crosses a line. A woman missing work or school every month deserves intervention even with a normal hemoglobin. Significant life impact means offering real treatment: a hormonal IUD, combined hormones, tranexamic acid, endometrial ablation, or fibroid-directed therapy, rather than watchful waiting. Document the impact because it justifies the intervention and gives you a concrete measure of response at follow-up.

history.question: Do you have cramping or pelvic pain with your periods? Headache, mood changes, or other symptoms around your period?
listenFor: Headache, mood, or other perimenstrual symptoms
history.meaning: Perimenstrual symptoms split the diagnosis. Severe cramping and pelvic pain that worsens over time point to endometriosis or adenomyosis, while cyclical headache and mood symptoms point to premenstrual disorders, and the two get completely different treatments. Severe dysmenorrhea earns a trial of NSAIDs plus hormonal suppression with a combined method or hormonal IUD, with laparoscopy referral if refractory or if infertility coexists. Cyclical mood symptoms meeting criteria respond to SSRIs given continuously or in the luteal phase. Menstrual migraine needs its own plan, and migraine with aura means avoiding estrogen-containing contraception because of stroke risk.

history.question: Any bleeding between periods? Any bleeding after sex?
history.meaning: Bleeding between periods or after sex is never just irregular periods; it points at the cervix or the endometrium, and postcoital bleeding in particular is the classic presentation of cervical pathology including cancer. The differential is cervical polyp, cervicitis, or cervical dysplasia and cancer versus endometrial polyp, hyperplasia, or endometrial cancer, with hormonal contraception as the common benign cause of breakthrough bleeding. Postcoital bleeding means a speculum exam and making sure cervical screening is current, with colposcopy if indicated; don't reassure without looking. Intermenstrual bleeding means transvaginal ultrasound for polyps or thickening and endometrial sampling if risk factors are present.

history.question: When did your periods stop? Any menopause symptoms? Any hormone therapy? Any bleeding or spotting since your periods stopped?
history.meaning: Any bleeding after twelve months of amenorrhea is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise; that rule drives everything here. The differential for postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer or hyperplasia, atrophic vaginitis, endometrial polyp, or hormone therapy effect. Postmenopausal bleeding gets a transvaginal ultrasound for endometrial thickness triage plus an endometrial biopsy, promptly rather than watched. Menopause timing and symptoms also frame hormone therapy counseling with clear discussion of risks and benefits, avoiding it with a history of breast cancer, clot, or stroke, plus bone health and calcium and vitamin D counseling.

history.question: Record: menarche age | LMP | cycle every __ days x __ days | flow | intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding Y/N.
history.meaning: A one-line menstrual summary with menarche, LMP, cycle interval and duration, flow, and intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding is handoff currency: it puts every future clinician on the same page and makes change over time visible at a glance. It forces completeness; if you can't fill the line, you haven't finished the history. Standardized documentation means a new change in flow or pattern gets caught at the next visit instead of buried in prose, and it lets you apply the PALM-COEIN framework systematically rather than from memory.

history.question: What is your GTPAL — gravida, term births, preterm births, abortions / losses / ectopics, living children?
history.meaning: GTPAL is the universal shorthand every OB clinician reads instantly: gravida, term births, preterm births, abortions and losses including ectopics, living children. Getting it right at the start frames every risk assessment that follows, from preterm birth risk to Rh management. A prior preterm birth triggers progesterone and cervical-length surveillance, prior losses mean ectopic vigilance and Rh attention, and grand multiparity raises the risk of postpartum hemorrhage and uterine atony, so you plan active management of the third stage with uterotonics ready.

history.question: For each pregnancy: what year, what gestational age, and what was the outcome?
history.meaning: The bare GTPAL number hides patterns, and the pattern is what changes management. Two preterm births at 32 weeks is a different story than one term and one preterm birth, and short interpregnancy intervals carry their own risks. Detailing each pregnancy by year, gestational age, and outcome distinguishes recurrent spontaneous preterm birth (cervical insufficiency versus indicated delivery) from sporadic events, and recurrent early loss (anatomic, genetic, antiphospholipid causes) from bad luck. Recurrent spontaneous preterm birth means progesterone, serial cervical lengths, and a cerclage discussion; recurrent loss means a formal recurrent-pregnancy-loss workup; short intervals mean contraception counseling postpartum.

history.question: Was labor spontaneous or induced? Was the delivery vaginal, operative vaginal, or cesarean?
history.meaning: How each labor started and ended predicts this pregnancy's labor. A prior cesarean raises the trial-of-labor versus repeat cesarean decision, while prior inductions or operative vaginal deliveries hint at dystocia or fetal intolerance of labor that may recur. A prior low-transverse cesarean means counseling on VBAC candidacy with its small but real uterine rupture risk; a prior classical cesarean means scheduled repeat with no labor. A prior operative vaginal delivery means anticipating possible recurrence of the indication and reassessing early rather than repeating the same difficult course.

history.question: What was the baby's sex and birth weight? Any maternal or newborn complications?
history.meaning: Birth weights flag recurrent growth problems: a prior macrosomic infant predicts gestational diabetes and shoulder dystocia, while a prior growth-restricted or NICU infant prompts closer fetal surveillance. Maternal complications like hemorrhage tend to recur as well. Prior macrosomia means early diabetes screening, estimated fetal weight surveillance, and delivery planning with the shoulder dystocia maneuvers team ready. Prior growth restriction means serial growth ultrasounds and antenatal testing starting in the third trimester, and prior postpartum hemorrhage means active third-stage management with blood typed and screened and uterotonics on hand.

history.question: Any pregnancy losses, ectopic pregnancies, or molar pregnancies — what type or cause, and was treatment medical or surgical? Any complications?
history.meaning: The type and management of each loss determines the workup. Recurrent early losses need evaluation for anatomic, genetic, and clotting causes; a prior ectopic markedly raises recurrence risk; and a prior molar pregnancy mandates hCG surveillance to zero with reliable contraception during the follow-up interval. Whether treatment was medical or surgical matters too. A prior ectopic means early first-trimester ultrasound to confirm intrauterine location rather than waiting for pain or bleeding; recurrent loss means a formal workup with karyotype, antiphospholipid panel, and uterine cavity evaluation; a prior molar pregnancy means early ultrasound in the next pregnancy and hCG follow-up.

history.question: Any of these complications in a prior pregnancy: preeclampsia or hypertension, gestational diabetes, preterm birth, fetal growth restriction, shoulder dystocia, postpartum hemorrhage, stillbirth or anomaly, blood clots, ICU stay, postpartum depression or psychosis?
history.meaning: Obstetric complications are among the most recurrent events in medicine, and this checklist directly generates the prevention plan; missing one means missing the intervention that prevents it. Prior preeclampsia means low-dose aspirin starting in the late first or early second trimester with close blood pressure surveillance; prior gestational diabetes means early glucose screening; prior preterm birth means progesterone and cervical-length monitoring. Prior stillbirth means antenatal testing and a delivery-timing discussion, prior postpartum hemorrhage means active third-stage management with blood available, prior clot means thromboprophylaxis assessment, and prior postpartum depression or psychosis means early screening with psychiatric follow-up and a safety plan in place.

history.question: How do you count a twin pregnancy in GTPAL?
listenFor: Each living child counted in L
history.meaning: GTPAL conventions are a classic source of handoff error: a twin pregnancy counts as one pregnancy in the G, T, P, and A counts, with each living child counted in L. Getting it wrong misrepresents parity and therefore risk, from grand multiparity hemorrhage risk to VBAC candidacy. When the numbers don't add up, clarify the convention out loud and use your institution's gestational-age threshold consistently so everyone reading the chart means the same thing.

history.question: Any pelvic or abdominal pain, vaginal discharge — its color, odor, consistency — itching or burning, vulvar lesions, or abnormal bleeding?
history.meaning: These symptoms localize the problem before you examine. Discharge with odor or itching points to bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, or candidiasis; vulvar lesions raise concern for herpes or HPV; pelvic pain suggests endometriosis, PID, or fibroids; and abnormal bleeding, especially postmenopausal, is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Discharge means wet mount or NAAT with treatment per guidelines and partner therapy for trich; lesions mean testing and treatment with biopsy if the diagnosis is uncertain. Abnormal bleeding means a pregnancy test, ultrasound, and endometrial sampling if risk factors are present, with postmenopausal bleeding worked up promptly rather than observed.

history.question: Any history of fibroids, endometriosis, ovarian cysts, PCOS, infertility, PID or STIs, or prolapse — how were they diagnosed and treated?
listenFor: Condition with diagnosis and treatment given
history.meaning: Prior diagnoses anchor the current differential: fibroids and endometriosis explain bleeding and pain patterns, PCOS explains irregular menses and metabolic risk, and PID history raises ectopic and infertility risk. Knowing how each was diagnosed and treated prevents repeating workups and flags recurrence versus a new problem. Known fibroids with new bleeding mean checking for growth on ultrasound rather than starting from scratch; PCOS means screening for diabetes and counseling on long-term metabolic risk; PID history means early pregnancy ultrasound to confirm intrauterine location and earlier infertility evaluation.

history.question: Any GYN procedures — biopsy, hysteroscopy or laparoscopy, ablation, myomectomy, hysterectomy, oophorectomy? What was the indication and date, and were there complications?
history.meaning: Procedures change anatomy and therefore change risk. A myomectomy that entered the uterine cavity means cesarean delivery with no labor; endometrial ablation makes future bleeding evaluation harder because of scarring; and hysterectomy or oophorectomy changes screening needs and hormone considerations. The indication and date tell you whether current symptoms are recurrence or something new. Bleeding after ablation needs hysteroscopy, not just ultrasound; a prior LEEP means cervical-length surveillance in pregnancy; and prior oophorectomy means addressing estrogen deficiency and bone health.

history.question: What are your pregnancy goals? How long have you been trying? Any prior fertility evaluation for you or your partner, or relevant disease or surgery?
history.meaning: Duration of trying defines infertility at twelve months, or six months if she's over 35, and triggers the evaluation pathway; asking about goals first keeps you from ordering a workup she doesn't want or missing one she needs. Prior evaluation for both partners avoids duplication. The differential splits into ovulatory causes like PCOS and thyroid disease, tubal factor from PID history, male factor, and unexplained. Meeting criteria means initiating the standard workup with ovulation assessment, semen analysis, and tubal patency testing, and referring to reproductive endocrinology rather than delaying; known barriers get addressed directly, such as ovulation induction for anovulation.

history.question: When was your last cervical cancer screening and what was the result? Any prior abnormal result or HPV, colposcopy, LEEP, or other treatment? Have you had HPV vaccination?
history.meaning: Screening history determines what's due and what the current risk is: a prior abnormal result or LEEP changes surveillance intervals and raises the stakes of new symptoms, while HPV vaccination modifies but doesn't eliminate the need for screening. New postcoital bleeding with overdue screening puts cervical dysplasia and cancer at the top of the differential. An overdue screen in a symptomatic patient gets expedited with colposcopy if indicated rather than routine scheduling; prior LEEP means following the intensified surveillance pathway and noting the cervical insufficiency risk in pregnancy. Document vaccination but continue age-appropriate screening.

history.question: When was your last mammogram or breast imaging and what was the result? Any current lump, pain, skin or nipple change, or discharge? Any prior breast biopsy, surgery, or cancer?
listenFor: Prior breast biopsy, surgery, or cancer
history.meaning: Screening history establishes baseline risk and what's due, while a current lump, skin or nipple change, or discharge needs prompt diagnostic imaging, not routine screening. Prior biopsy or cancer markedly changes the surveillance plan. A new lump splits by age and features into fibroadenoma, cyst, or cancer; bloody unilateral nipple discharge raises concern for intraductal papilloma or malignancy. Current concerning symptoms mean diagnostic mammogram plus targeted ultrasound promptly, with biopsy for suspicious findings; prior atypia or cancer means a high-risk surveillance pathway with MRI considered per guidelines.

history.question: Any burning with urination or urinating more often? Any urine leakage with coughing, sneezing, or exercise (stress) versus a sudden urge you cannot hold (urge)?
history.meaning: The stress-versus-urge distinction determines treatment. Stress leakage with cough, sneeze, or exercise is anatomic, a support failure treated with pelvic floor muscle training first and surgical options like a midurethral sling if bothersome. Urge leakage with a sudden unholdable urge is detrusor overactivity, treated with behavioral therapy and bladder training first, then medication. Dysuria or frequency separately suggests UTI, overactive bladder, or atrophic vaginitis and needs a urinalysis and culture before treatment. Mixed incontinence means treating the predominant and most bothersome component first.

history.question: Any stool or gas leakage, constipation, pelvic pressure, or a vaginal bulge?
history.meaning: Fecal or gas leakage, pelvic pressure, and a vaginal bulge point to pelvic organ prolapse or pelvic floor dysfunction: common, underreported, and very treatable. Constipation is both a symptom and a driver, since chronic straining worsens prolapse. The differential includes uterine or vault prolapse, cystocele, and rectocele, with fecal incontinence suggesting obstetric sphincter injury or age-related sphincter weakness. Symptomatic prolapse gets graded on exam and managed from pessary to surgical repair based on severity and patient goals; fecal incontinence means a bowel regimen, pelvic floor therapy, and urogynecology or colorectal referral; and constipation gets treated aggressively as part of prolapse management.

history.question: I ask everyone these questions because sexual health is part of overall health. Is it okay if we discuss this?
history.meaning: Explicitly normalizing the topic and asking permission is what gets honest answers; patients disclose more when sensitive questions are framed as routine rather than judgmental. If she declines, pushing destroys trust, so you respect it, document, and revisit at a later visit rather than skipping the history entirely. Better disclosure directly changes testing and counseling: more STIs found, more contraception needs identified, more safety concerns surfaced. The permission statement is a clinical tool, not just politeness.

history.question: Are you having sex of any kind now or in the past? How many partners in recent months? What genders? Any new or concurrent partners?
history.meaning: Partner number, genders, and concurrency define STI and HIV risk far better than assumptions about orientation or relationship status; a monogamous patient with a non-monogamous partner carries the partner's risk. New or concurrent partners are the strongest behavioral predictors of incident STI. This risk stratification drives testing: new, multiple, or concurrent partners mean offering comprehensive STI screening including HIV and syphilis, plus hepatitis screening per risk. It also determines partner notification and treatment if an STI is found, since treating only the patient guarantees reinfection.

history.question: What kinds of sex — oral, vaginal/frontal, anal — and which body parts are involved?
history.meaning: You can't order the right tests without knowing the exposures, because genital-only testing misses extragenital infections. Oral sex needs throat screening and anal sex needs rectal screening; pharyngeal gonorrhea and rectal chlamydia are often asymptomatic and invisible to urine testing alone. Order NAAT at each exposed site: genital, pharyngeal, and rectal as indicated. Counsel that barriers apply to oral and anal sex too, not just vaginal, since patients often reserve condoms for pregnancy prevention alone.

history.question: Do you use condoms or barriers — for which acts and how often? Any STI testing? Have you had HPV or hepatitis vaccines? Is PrEP relevant?
history.meaning: Detailing barrier use by act reveals the actual protection gaps: condoms used inconsistently or only for vaginal sex leave major risk uncovered. Testing and vaccine history show what's missing, and this is also where PrEP candidacy gets identified. Inconsistent barrier use means counseling on correct consistent use and offering alternatives; due HPV or hepatitis vaccines mean vaccinating now. Substantial HIV risk, such as a partner with HIV, inconsistent condom use, or a recent STI, means offering PrEP with HIV testing. Even patients who aren't sexually active still need age-appropriate cervical screening.

history.question: Any past STIs — testing and prior diagnoses, dates, treatment, recurrence, partner history? Ask specifically as needed: gonorrhea, chlamydia, trich, HSV, HPV/warts, syphilis, HIV, hepatitis, PID.
history.meaning: A prior STI is the strongest predictor of a current or future one, marking both ongoing risk and biological susceptibility, and PID history specifically predicts tubal damage. The details matter: what it was, when, whether it was treated, and whether partners were treated tells you if this is treatment failure, reinfection from an untreated partner, or a new infection. Prior STI means retesting now, confirming partners were treated with expedited partner therapy where appropriate, and counseling on condoms. PID history means early pregnancy ultrasound to confirm intrauterine location given the ectopic risk, and earlier infertility evaluation; prior syphilis means checking titers to distinguish treated from active disease.

history.question: Would you like pregnancy now, later, or not at all? How important is preventing pregnancy? What contraception do you use now or used before — adherence, satisfaction, side effects?
listenFor: Pregnancy intention and contraception history given
history.meaning: Clarifying intention first, whether she wants pregnancy now, later, or not at all, keeps counseling aligned with her actual goals instead of your assumptions. Asking about adherence, satisfaction, and side effects uncovers why a method is failing, which is more useful than refilling the same prescription. Adherence problems with a desire to avoid pregnancy mean switching to a method that fits her life, such as long-acting reversible contraception; side effects mean switching method class rather than abandoning contraception. Wanting pregnancy soon means preconception counseling with folic acid, chronic disease optimization, and teratogen review; ambivalence means offering decision support without pressure.

history.question: Any pain with sex? Any concerns about desire, arousal, orgasm, pleasure, or satisfaction? Any unwanted or coerced sexual activity?
history.meaning: Patients almost never volunteer sexual pain, dysfunction, or coercion, so you have to ask directly. Dyspareunia has real medical causes including endometriosis, infection, vulvodynia, and atrophy, and any disclosure of coercion turns the visit into a safety encounter. Dyspareunia means a targeted exam and workup: treat infection, evaluate for endometriosis, address atrophy with estrogen. Dysfunction means reviewing medications, since SSRIs are a classic cause, with counseling and therapy referral as indicated. Coercion disclosed means a private supportive response, safety planning, and social work and community resources, documented carefully and with her consent.

history.question: When appropriate, interview alone. Do you feel safe at home and in your relationships? Has anyone hurt, threatened, controlled you, or forced you into sexual activity?
history.meaning: Abuse hides behind a present partner, so asking with the partner in the room guarantees a no; interviewing alone is the only way disclosure happens. Pregnancy is a high-risk period for escalation of violence, and intimate partner violence directly worsens maternal and fetal outcomes. A disclosure means safety planning, social work involvement, and community resources like hotlines and shelters, documented objectively and with her consent. It changes obstetric management too: closer follow-up, recognizing missed visits as a possible control tactic, and trauma-informed care through labor.

history.question: Any family history of breast, ovarian, endometrial/uterine, cervical, or colon cancer — which relative and at what age? Any blood clots or osteoporosis?
history.meaning: Early-onset breast, ovarian, endometrial, or colon cancer in the family suggests hereditary syndromes like BRCA or Lynch that change screening, prevention, and referral; clot history determines whether estrogen contraception is safe. Which relative and what age is what makes the pattern recognizable, distinguishing BRCA from Lynch from Cowden patterns by the cancer mix. A concerning pattern means referring for genetic counseling and testing; high risk means earlier and more intensive screening such as breast MRI or earlier colonoscopy. Clot history means avoiding estrogen-containing contraception in favor of progestin-only or non-hormonal options, and osteoporosis history means bone-health counseling.

history.question: If pregnancy-relevant: any known inherited disorders, developmental delay, trisomy, neural tube defects, or congenital heart defects in the family?
history.meaning: A family history of chromosomal conditions, neural tube defects, or congenital heart disease changes prenatal care, but only if you elicit it before or early in pregnancy while there's still time to act. This is one of the few history questions with a narrow window of usefulness. Neural tube defect history means high-dose folic acid starting preconception; known carrier risks mean offering carrier screening and genetic counseling; congenital heart disease in the family means a fetal echocardiogram. Adjust aneuploidy screening counseling based on the specific history rather than giving the standard spiel.

history.question: What hormones or contraceptives, blood thinners, fertility medications, over-the-counter drugs, herbs, or vitamins do you take?
history.meaning: Patients don't volunteer herbals, supplements, and over-the-counter drugs, but they interact, bleed, and harm fetuses just as much as prescriptions do. Hormones, anticoagulants, and fertility drugs each carry specific OB/GYN implications. Identify teratogens and switch them before or in early pregnancy: ACE inhibitors, certain antiepileptics, retinoids. Anticoagulants need a plan around delivery and neuraxial anesthesia, and herbals need a frank conversation that natural doesn't mean safe in pregnancy. Reconcile the full list before prescribing anything new.

history.question: Do you use tobacco, alcohol, cannabis, or other drugs?
history.meaning: Tobacco, alcohol, and drugs directly worsen pregnancy outcomes: alcohol causes fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, smoking drives growth restriction and abruption, and stimulants raise abruption and preterm birth risk. Use also shapes contraceptive choices and counseling. Asked nonjudgmentally, the question opens the door to help; asked judgmentally, it closes it. Any use in pregnancy means brief counseling, cessation resources, and referral to treatment programs, with adjusted surveillance such as growth ultrasounds for smoking or stimulant use. Postpartum, counsel on breastfeeding and substance use and arrange ongoing support, documenting the help offered rather than the judgment.

history.question: Any allergies, including latex — and what was the reaction?
history.meaning: Latex is everywhere in OB/GYN: gloves, condoms, catheters, diaphragms, so a latex allergy is a procedural landmine. The specific reaction separates true allergy with hives or anaphylaxis from irritation or contact dermatitis, and that distinction determines how aggressively you avoid it. True latex allergy means flagging the chart prominently and using latex-free gloves and equipment for every exam and delivery, with anesthesia aware for catheters and drains. Drug allergies mean choosing alternatives for GBS prophylaxis, surgical prophylaxis, and labor medications. Document the reaction type, not just the allergen name.

history.question: What else about your menstrual, reproductive, or sexual health should we discuss today?
history.meaning: The structured questions never catch everything, and patients routinely save their real concern for last: the thing they were embarrassed to raise or that didn't fit your boxes. This question surfaces the actual reason for the visit more often than you'd expect. Whatever comes up gets addressed or scheduled, whether it's dyspareunia, incontinence, or a fertility worry, and it often reframes the visit plan entirely. Never skip it when time is short, because that's exactly when the important thing gets missed.

history.question: One-liner: ___-year-old G__P____ at __w__d (if pregnant), LMP ___, presenting with ___. Key menstrual, OB, GYN, and sexual history: ___.
history.meaning: The one-liner is handoff currency: age, gravidity and parity, gestational age, and the key history in one breath so anyone picking up the chart grasps the essentials in seconds. Building it forces you to decide what actually matters, which is itself a clinical reasoning exercise; if you can't write it cleanly, you haven't finished thinking. A sharp one-liner makes sign-out, consults, and triage decisions faster and safer, so go back and find the story when the pieces don't fit.

history.question: When did the tightening or cramping start, and how far apart are the contractions right now? How long does each one last?
history.meaning: Timing separates true labor from look-alikes. Regular contractions that are getting closer together and lasting longer point to true preterm labor, while irregular tightening that eases with rest or fluids is classic for Braxton-Hicks contractions or an irritable uterus. The main differentials here are true preterm labor versus false labor, dehydration-related cramping, and urinary tract infection. If the pattern is regular and persistent before 37 weeks, she needs a full preterm labor workup on triage (timed contractions, cervical assessment, fetal fibronectin or cervical length) and you start thinking about admission, antenatal steroids, and tocolysis; if irregular and unchanged, hydration and observation are usually enough.

history.question: Are the contractions painful, and are they getting stronger, longer, or closer together over time?
history.meaning: Progression is what defines labor: contractions that intensify and cluster mean the uterus is organizing toward delivery, while painless or fading contractions suggest false labor. This helps distinguish true preterm labor from Braxton-Hicks contractions, round ligament pain, and GI cramping. Progressive, painful, regular contractions before 37 weeks push you toward admission with tocolysis candidacy (for example nifedipine) plus steroids if under 34 weeks; non-progressive contractions let you observe, hydrate, and discharge with return precautions instead.

history.question: Have you felt any gush or steady trickle of fluid leaking from your vagina?
history.meaning: Fluid leak means possible preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM), which completely changes the plan. The differentials are PPROM versus urinary incontinence, increased vaginal discharge, or a small leak that already sealed. If membranes may be ruptured you must avoid digital cervical exams (they seed infection and shorten latency), start GBS prophylaxis, give latency antibiotics if under 34 weeks, give steroids if under 34 weeks, admit, and call for NICU input; if there is no leak you keep the standard preterm labor workup with digital exams allowed.

history.question: Any vaginal bleeding or spotting? If so, how much — spotting, like a period, or with clots?
history.meaning: Bleeding sorts bloody show of early labor from dangerous causes. Light spotting with cramping can be the bloody show of cervical change, but heavier bleeding raises placental abruption and placenta previa, and abruption itself can trigger preterm contractions. Bleeding is a hard stop for tocolysis: you do not give nifedipine to someone who may be abrupting, because tocolysis can mask a worsening abruption and delay a needed delivery. Heavy bleeding or suspected abruption means continuous monitoring, type and crossmatch, and preparing for possible urgent delivery instead of trying to stop labor.

history.question: How is the baby moving compared to usual?
history.meaning: Fetal movement is the fastest bedside screen for fetal well-being. Normal movement is reassuring, while decreased movement raises concern for fetal compromise from uteroplacental insufficiency, oligohydramnios after membrane rupture, or early infection. Decreased movement changes management immediately: you move to continuous fetal monitoring and a biophysical profile or nonstress test, and a nonreassuring pattern can force delivery even at a preterm gestational age rather than continuing tocolysis.

history.question: Do you feel new pelvic pressure, like the baby is pushing down, or a dull low backache that comes and goes?
history.meaning: New pelvic pressure suggests the presenting part is descending against a changing cervix, and rhythmic low back pain can be posterior preterm labor rather than musculoskeletal strain. The differentials are cervical change and descent versus constipation, back strain, and urinary infection. Pressure or rhythmic backache with contractions strengthens the case for true preterm labor and pushes you toward a cervical exam (if membranes are intact), admission, and steroids; without it you lean more toward observation.

history.question: Any fever, chills, burning when you pee, or foul-smelling vaginal discharge?
history.meaning: Infection is both a trigger and a contraindication. Urinary tract infection and pyelonephritis commonly provoke preterm contractions, and fever with uterine tenderness raises chorioamnionitis, especially if membranes are ruptured. Chorioamnionitis is an absolute contraindication to tocolysis: you do not try to stop labor in an infected uterus, because prolonging it endangers mother and baby. Fever or infectious symptoms redirect you to cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and delivery rather than nifedipine and steroids-for-latency.

history.question: What is your due date, and how was it set — a first-trimester ultrasound or your last period?
history.meaning: Every management threshold in preterm labor is gestational-age driven: antenatal steroids below 34 weeks, magnesium for fetal neuroprotection below 32 weeks, and viability counseling around 24 weeks. First-trimester ultrasound dating is the most reliable; last-period dating can be off by weeks if cycles were irregular. If dating is uncertain you confirm it before committing to steroids, tocolysis, or delivery decisions, because treating at the wrong gestational age means either missing a beneficial therapy or intervening unnecessarily.

history.question: What is your GBS status — were you screened, and was the result positive?
history.meaning: Group B strep status determines intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Anyone in preterm labor who is GBS positive, or whose status is unknown (screening usually happens at 36 weeks, so most preterm patients are unknown), needs prophylactic antibiotics in labor to prevent early-onset neonatal sepsis. A negative screen is the only result that lets you skip it. Knowing the answer at triage means the antibiotic order goes in with admission instead of being missed.

history.question: Have you already had the steroid shots for the baby's lungs (betamethasone) during this pregnancy?
history.meaning: One course of antenatal corticosteroids between 24 and 34 weeks accelerates fetal lung maturity and lowers neonatal respiratory distress, brain bleeds, and death. If she has not received them and delivery looks possible, you give the first dose now without delay, because benefit accrues quickly and the window closes once she delivers. If a full course was already completed weeks ago, a single rescue course may be considered if preterm birth again looks imminent; documenting prior dosing prevents both missing the therapy and giving unnecessary repeat courses.

history.question: When was your last cervical exam, and what did it show?
history.meaning: A prior exam gives you the baseline that makes the current exam meaningful: cervical change over time is the definition of labor. It also tells you whether membranes were documented intact, which determines whether a repeat digital exam is safe now. If the last exam was recent and unchanged, you may lean on cervical length or fibronectin instead of repeating a digital exam; if she was already dilating, you move faster toward admission and steroids.

history.question: Tell me about your prior pregnancies — how many births, any preterm deliveries, miscarriages, or C-sections?
history.meaning: This is the GTPAL history, and a prior spontaneous preterm birth is the strongest predictor of another one, which raises your pretest probability that these contractions are the real thing. Prior C-section matters because if preterm delivery becomes necessary, the uterine scar constrains your options for induction and vaginal birth. A history of recurrent preterm birth also flags her for progesterone prophylaxis counseling after this pregnancy, and for closer surveillance in future pregnancies.

history.question: What medications do you take, and do you have any drug allergies?
history.meaning: The medication list screens for tocolytic interactions and contraindications: for example, nifedipine interacts with other antihypertensives and is avoided with certain cardiac conditions, and magnesium needs caution in renal disease. A penicillin allergy directly changes GBS prophylaxis, since the default intrapartum penicillin must be swapped for an alternative based on allergy severity and susceptibilities. Getting this at triage avoids a delayed or wrong antibiotic order when labor progresses.

history.question: Do you smoke, drink alcohol, or use any other substances?
history.meaning: Smoking and substance use are modifiable risk factors for preterm birth and placental abruption, so a positive answer sharpens your counseling and your suspicion for abruption if bleeding appears. It also matters for the neonate: certain exposures change newborn withdrawal monitoring and pediatric planning. A positive screen triggers social work and cessation resources rather than judgment, and it documents risk factors that explain recurrence risk.

exam.maneuver: Take full vital signs: blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, respiratory rate, and pulse oximetry.
exam.meaning: Vitals screen for the two conditions that override the preterm labor plan. Fever plus tachycardia points toward chorioamnionitis or pyelonephritis, which makes tocolysis unsafe and pivots you to antibiotics and delivery. Severe-range blood pressure raises preeclampsia with severe features, where the treatment is delivery and magnesium for seizure prophylaxis, not stopping contractions. Normal vitals keep the standard preterm labor pathway open.

exam.maneuver: Measure fundal height in centimeters from pubic symphysis to uterine fundus.
exam.meaning: Fundal height is a rough check on dating and amniotic fluid. Measuring much smaller than dates raises oligohydramnios (suggesting ruptured membranes with fluid loss) or fetal growth restriction, while much larger suggests polyhydramnios or wrong dates. A size-date mismatch makes you question the gestational age you are basing steroid and tocolysis decisions on, and oligohydramnios with contractions strengthens the case for PPROM workup.

exam.maneuver: Perform Leopold maneuvers to determine fetal lie, presentation, and position.
exam.meaning: You need to know how the baby is lying before labor advances, because malpresentation changes the delivery plan entirely. A cephalic baby keeps vaginal delivery on the table; a breech or transverse baby at a viable preterm gestation usually means cesarean if delivery becomes necessary, and a transverse lie with ruptured membranes is an emergency. Finding malpresentation early also triggers consideration of external cephalic version candidacy and changes how urgently you involve the attending.

exam.maneuver: Palpate the uterus continuously for 10 minutes, timing contraction frequency and duration and feeling resting tone between contractions.
findings: Uterus never fully relaxes between contractions
exam.meaning: Hands-on palpation documents the contraction pattern objectively instead of relying on the patient's report. Regular, palpable contractions with a soft resting tone support true preterm labor and admission for tocolysis evaluation; irregular tightening supports false labor and observation. A uterus that never relaxes (hypertonus) or contractions coming too frequently raise abruption, which is a contraindication to tocolysis and a reason to prepare for delivery.

exam.maneuver: Place on continuous fetal heart rate monitoring and assess baseline, variability, accelerations, and decelerations.
exam.meaning: The tracing tells you whether the fetus is tolerating the contractions. A reassuring tracing lets you continue the preterm labor workup and consider tocolysis; recurrent decelerations or minimal variability mean a nonreassuring fetal status that can force delivery regardless of gestational age. Fetal tachycardia is an early flag for chorioamnionitis, which would cancel tocolysis plans and start antibiotics. Monitoring stays on until the clinical picture is stable.

exam.maneuver: If rupture of membranes is suspected, do a sterile speculum exam: look for pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix, test ferning on dried fluid, and check nitrazine paper.
exam.meaning: The speculum exam confirms or excludes PPROM, which forks the entire management tree. Pooling, ferning, and alkaline nitrazine together are classic for ruptured membranes; a dry vault with negative tests points back to intact membranes and the standard preterm labor pathway. A confirmed rupture means no digital exams, admission, GBS prophylaxis, latency antibiotics under 34 weeks, steroids under 34 weeks, and NICU involvement, so this exam directly triggers that cascade.

exam.maneuver: Do NOT perform a digital cervical exam when PPROM is possible or confirmed; document that the digital exam was deferred and why.
exam.meaning: Withholding the digital exam is itself the intervention. Digital exams push vaginal bacteria upward, shorten the latency period before delivery, and raise the risk of chorioamnionitis and neonatal sepsis without adding information you cannot get from the speculum exam. The plan changes accordingly: cervical assessment relies on speculum visualization and transvaginal cervical length instead, and every clinician on the team needs to see the deferral documented so no one repeats it.

exam.maneuver: If membranes are intact, perform a digital cervical exam: dilation, effacement, station, position, and consistency.
findings: Dilated and effacing with station noted
exam.meaning: With intact membranes the digital exam is safe and is the test that defines labor: documented cervical change over time plus regular contractions equals preterm labor. A closed, long cervix argues against true labor and supports observation or discharge, while dilation with effacement triggers admission, steroids if under 34 weeks, and tocolysis consideration. Station also tells you how imminent delivery is, which affects whether there is time for a full steroid course and whether NICU needs to be at the bedside.

exam.maneuver: Collect fetal fibronectin from vaginal secretions if she is 24 to 34 weeks with intact membranes and minimal dilation.
exam.meaning: Fetal fibronectin is a rule-out test for imminent preterm delivery. A negative result strongly predicts she will not deliver in the next 7 to 14 days, which lets you avoid admission, tocolysis, and steroids in someone with equivocal contractions. A positive result does not guarantee delivery but raises the risk enough to admit, give steroids, and consider tocolysis. The test is only valid with intact membranes and before significant dilation, so timing and technique matter.

exam.maneuver: Measure cervical length by transvaginal ultrasound.
exam.meaning: Cervical length is the anatomic counterpart to fibronectin: a long cervix in a symptomatic patient predicts she is unlikely to deliver soon, supporting discharge with precautions, while a short cervix (under 25 mm) marks high risk for preterm birth and supports admission, steroids, and tocolysis. Unlike a digital exam it is safe even when rupture is a question, and it gives an objective number to follow on serial exams. A short cervix also prompts discussion of NICU consultation and possible maternal transfer to a higher-level center if delivery looks likely at an early gestation.

history.question: When exactly did you first notice fluid leaking, and has it continued since then?
listenFor: Leaking on and off for hours
history.meaning: Timing of rupture sets the latency clock: the longer membranes have been ruptured, the higher the infection risk, and prolonged rupture changes antibiotic and delivery planning. A single small leak that stopped may be a hindwater leak that sealed, which carries a different prognosis than ongoing rupture. The differentials are true membrane rupture versus urinary incontinence and heavy vaginal discharge. A clear timeline anchors decisions about latency antibiotics, steroids, and when expectant management is no longer safe.

history.question: What color was the fluid — clear like water, green or brown, or bloody?
history.meaning: Color tells you about fetal status and bleeding. Clear fluid is the baseline; green or brown staining means meconium, which suggests fetal stress and changes neonatal resuscitation planning since the pediatric team must be ready at delivery. Bloody fluid raises placental abruption or a bleeding placenta previa, both of which push toward delivery rather than expectant management. Color alone can therefore move the plan from watchful waiting to preparing for birth.

history.question: Does the leaking fluid have any smell?
history.meaning: Odor screens for infection. Foul-smelling fluid is classic for chorioamnionitis, which is one of the hard indications to deliver regardless of gestational age, because prolonging a pregnancy in an infected uterus endangers mother and baby. A urine-like smell points instead toward incontinence, which would take membrane rupture off the table. Foul odor triggers maternal vitals, fundal tenderness exam, labs, and broad-spectrum antibiotics rather than continued expectant management.

history.question: Was it a big gush all at once, or more of a steady trickle — and are you still leaking now?
history.meaning: Amount and ongoing leakage help confirm rupture and estimate fluid loss. A dramatic gush followed by continuous leaking is classic for membrane rupture, while a one-time dampness without recurrence is more consistent with incontinence or discharge. Ongoing leakage also matters because persistent oligohydramnios raises the risk of cord compression and fetal distress, which shows up as variable decelerations on monitoring and can force delivery.

history.question: Have you had any contractions, cramping, or tightening since the fluid started?
history.meaning: Contractions after rupture signal that labor may be starting, which shortens the expected latency period and moves you toward delivery planning. No contractions with confirmed rupture supports expectant management at preterm gestations, buying time for steroids and antibiotics to work. The differential is spontaneous labor onset versus uterine irritability from infection, since chorioamnionitis can also provoke contractions — fever plus contractions after rupture should make you evaluate for infection rather than assuming normal labor.

history.question: Any fever, chills, or feeling flu-like since your water broke?
history.meaning: Fever after membrane rupture is chorioamnionitis until proven otherwise, and it is the single finding that most urgently ends expectant management. The differentials are intrauterine infection versus urinary tract infection versus a viral illness, but with ruptured membranes the uterus is the presumed source. Fever triggers a full infection workup, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and delivery regardless of gestational age, because the infected intrauterine environment harms both mother and fetus the longer it continues.

history.question: How is the baby moving compared to usual?
history.meaning: After rupture, decreased movement can reflect oligohydramnios with cord compression or early fetal compromise from infection. Normal movement is reassuring and supports continued expectant management at preterm gestations. Decreased movement changes the plan to continuous monitoring and biophysical assessment, and a nonreassuring pattern means delivery even if the gestational age would otherwise favor waiting.

history.question: What is your due date — how many weeks pregnant are you right now?
history.meaning: Gestational age is the entire management fork for ruptured membranes. At 37 weeks or beyond, the answer is delivery, usually induction, because the risks of waiting exceed any benefit. Between 34 weeks and 36 weeks 6 days, expectant management and delivery are both reasonable and the decision weighs infection risk against neonatal maturity, with GBS prophylaxis either way. Below 34 weeks, expectant management is preferred with latency antibiotics, antenatal steroids, and magnesium for neuroprotection under 32 weeks, since each day gained meaningfully improves neonatal outcomes.

history.question: What is your GBS status — screened and positive, negative, or unknown?
history.meaning: Ruptured membranes plus labor is the setup for early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis, so prophylaxis is mandatory for anyone positive or unknown. Most patients with PPROM have not reached the 36-week screening yet, so unknown status is the common scenario and still gets treated. A documented negative screen is the only result that avoids intrapartum antibiotics. Getting the answer at triage means prophylaxis starts with admission instead of after delivery is already underway.

history.question: Any prior pregnancies with ruptured membranes, preterm birth, or C-section?
history.meaning: Prior PPROM or preterm birth raises the likelihood of recurrence and of a short latency period this time, which makes you watch more closely for labor onset and infection. A prior C-section constrains delivery options: if induction or delivery becomes necessary, the scarred uterus changes the counseling around induction agents and the threshold for repeat cesarean. This history also informs whether she needs a higher-level center if delivery looks likely at an early gestation.

history.question: What medications do you take, and any drug allergies, especially penicillin?
history.meaning: Latency antibiotics and GBS prophylaxis both hinge on this answer. The standard latency regimen and intrapartum GBS prophylaxis are penicillin-based, so a reported allergy forces you to clarify severity and choose an alternative guided by susceptibilities. The medication list also flags anticoagulants or other drugs that complicate delivery planning. Sorting this out at triage prevents a delayed first antibiotic dose, and timing of the first dose matters for neonatal protection.

history.question: Do you smoke or use any tobacco, alcohol, or other substances?
history.meaning: Smoking is a risk factor for membrane rupture and abruption, so a positive answer fits the clinical picture and sharpens counseling about recurrence. Substance use can affect neonatal planning, including withdrawal monitoring. Beyond risk stratification, this question opens the door to cessation resources and social work support, which are part of comprehensive preterm care rather than an afterthought.

exam.maneuver: Take vital signs with careful attention to temperature, heart rate, and blood pressure.
exam.meaning: Temperature is the vital sign that matters most after rupture: fever is the cardinal sign of chorioamnionitis and immediately ends expectant management in favor of antibiotics and delivery. Maternal tachycardia can be an earlier or accompanying sign of infection. Normal vitals keep the gestational-age-based plan (expectant versus delivery) intact, but vitals must be rechecked frequently because chorioamnionitis can declare itself hours after rupture.

exam.maneuver: Palpate the uterus for fundal tenderness, noting whether the uterus is soft or tender between contractions.
exam.meaning: Fundal tenderness is a bedside hallmark of chorioamnionitis, often appearing alongside fever and fetal tachycardia. A soft, nontender uterus supports continued expectant management at preterm gestations. Tenderness changes everything: it triggers the infection workup, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and delivery regardless of gestational age, because an infected uterus should be emptied rather than watched.

exam.maneuver: Perform a sterile speculum exam and look for pooling of fluid in the posterior fornix; ask her to cough or bear down to provoke leaking.
findings: Fluid seen leaking from the cervical os
exam.meaning: Pooling is the most direct visual confirmation of ruptured membranes. Seeing fluid well up from the os with Valsalva is diagnostic and commits you to the rupture pathway: admission, GBS prophylaxis, and gestational-age-based management. A dry vault with no pooling despite the history suggests the leak sealed or was never rupture, which can return you to the preterm labor workup with digital exams permitted. The speculum exam must be sterile to avoid introducing infection into an already vulnerable space.

exam.maneuver: Test ferning: let collected fluid air-dry on a slide and examine for a fern-like crystallization pattern.
exam.meaning: Ferning confirms the fluid is amniotic: the salt and protein content of amniotic fluid crystallizes into a fern pattern as it dries, while urine and most discharge do not. A positive fern with pooling nails the diagnosis of rupture. A negative fern with a convincing history does not fully exclude rupture (the sample may be scant or contaminated), so you interpret it alongside pooling and nitrazine rather than in isolation.

exam.maneuver: Test nitrazine paper against the fluid; amniotic fluid is alkaline and turns the paper blue.
exam.meaning: Nitrazine is the third leg of the bedside confirmation trio with pooling and ferning. Amniotic fluid is alkaline while normal vaginal secretions are acidic, so a blue change supports rupture. False positives occur with blood, semen, or bacterial vaginosis, and false negatives with scant fluid, so nitrazine is interpreted together with pooling and ferning, never alone. Concordant positives across the tests give you the confidence to commit to the rupture management pathway.

exam.maneuver: Do NOT perform a digital cervical exam; document that it was deferred because of suspected or confirmed rupture.
findings: Deferral documented and communicated to team
exam.meaning: This is a deliberate omission and one of the highest-yield decisions in PPROM care. Digital exams inoculate the lower genital tract flora upward, shorten the latency period to delivery, and increase chorioamnionitis and neonatal sepsis without changing management, since cervical status does not alter the rupture plan.
