history.meaning: Cervical cancer is preventable when screening stays on schedule: cytology every 3 years from 21 to 29, then HPV-based testing — co-testing every 5 years or primary HPV — from 30 to 65; mammography starts at 40 and colorectal screening at 45. Knowing her status tells you what to do today: an overdue Pap gets collected at this visit, an overdue mammogram or colon screening gets ordered, and a prior high-grade abnormality needs confirmation that colposcopy follow-up was completed.

history.question: Are you using contraception, and is it working for you — or would you like something different?
history.meaning: Satisfaction predicts continuation, and discontinuation without a backup plan is how unintended pregnancies happen. This question uncovers side effects she may not volunteer — breakthrough bleeding, mood changes, weight gain — that point to a better method fit. If she is unhappy, counsel across the full range including long-acting reversible methods; if she wants to conceive soon, start preconception counseling and folic acid.

history.question: Are you sexually active? With men, women, or both — how many partners in the past year, and do you use condoms?
history.meaning: Partner number, partner gender, and condom use determine STI risk and which prevention counseling applies. New or multiple partners and inconsistent condom use raise the risk of chlamydia, gonorrhea, trichomoniasis, and HIV. Higher risk triggers NAAT screening for chlamydia and gonorrhea plus an HIV screen, condom counseling, and a discussion of PrEP when indicated.

history.question: Are you having hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, or new trouble sleeping?
history.meaning: Vasomotor and genitourinary symptoms mark the menopause transition and are treatable, while thyroid disease and depression can mimic them. Bothersome hot flashes open a discussion of hormone therapy risks and benefits or non-hormonal options; vaginal dryness responds to vaginal estrogen. This is also the moment for bone health counseling — calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise — and planning bone density screening at 65, earlier with risk factors.

history.question: How many times have you been pregnant, and what happened with each — live births, miscarriages, or terminations?
history.meaning: Gravidity and parity shape both counseling and risk: nulliparity modestly raises ovarian and endometrial cancer risk, and prior pregnancy complications predict future ones. A history of preeclampsia, preterm birth, or gestational diabetes changes preconception planning — including low-dose aspirin in a future pregnancy after preeclampsia. Recurrent loss warrants a workup and referral rather than reassurance alone.

history.question: What prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, and supplements do you take? Any drug allergies?
history.meaning: Enzyme-inducing drugs like carbamazepine blunt hormonal contraception, and teratogenic drugs matter the moment pregnancy is possible. A complete list lets you catch interactions before prescribing. If she takes an interacting drug, switch the contraceptive method or the drug; document allergies now so any procedure or prescription later is safe.

history.question: Over the past two weeks, have you felt down or hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually enjoy? Have you felt anxious or on edge?
history.meaning: Depression and anxiety are common, under-detected, and directly affect whether she follows through on screening and treatment plans. Thyroid disease and substance use can mimic both, so keep the differential open. A positive screen leads to a PHQ-9 or GAD-7, a safety assessment, and referral or treatment — with same-day urgent evaluation if she endorses self-harm.

history.question: Do you feel safe in your relationships and at home? Has anyone ever hurt, threatened, or frightened you?
history.meaning: Intimate partner violence affects a large share of women and rarely gets disclosed without a direct question asked in private. A positive or evasive answer shifts the visit toward safety: assess immediate danger, offer shelter and hotline resources, and document carefully. Never confront the partner, and follow your jurisdiction's reporting requirements.

history.question: Do you smoke or vape, drink alcohol, or use marijuana or other recreational drugs?
history.meaning: Tobacco raises cervical, breast, and cardiovascular risk and undermines estrogen-containing contraception after 35; alcohol and drug use affect pregnancy planning and cancer risk. Any use opens brief cessation counseling and quitline referral. If she is considering pregnancy, this becomes preconception counseling on abstinence from alcohol.

history.question: Has anyone in your family had breast, ovarian, uterine, or colon cancer — especially at a young age? Has anyone been tested for BRCA or Lynch syndrome?
history.meaning: Early-onset breast or ovarian cancer, male breast cancer, or multiple affected relatives point to BRCA1/2, while young colon or endometrial cancer points to Lynch syndrome. These red flags change management from routine screening to genetic counseling and testing referral, which can trigger earlier mammograms, breast MRI, or risk-reducing surgery discussions.

history.question: Are your vaccines current — the HPV series, yearly flu shot, COVID, and Tdap within the last 10 years?
listenFor: finished HPV shots as a teen
history.meaning: HPV vaccination prevents the infections that cause cervical cancer and is recommended through age 45 for those not previously vaccinated; flu, COVID, and Tdap protect her now and in any future pregnancy. Gaps found today get filled today: offer the HPV series if incomplete, give flu and COVID if due, and give Tdap if she has not had one in 10 years.

exam.maneuver: Record blood pressure, heart rate, and BMI
exam.meaning: Blood pressure catches undiagnosed hypertension, which changes contraceptive prescribing — combined estrogen methods are off the table with uncontrolled hypertension or migraine with aura. BMI guides counseling on diabetes screening and weight management. An elevated reading gets repeated and worked up rather than ignored.

exam.maneuver: Palpate the thyroid for size, nodules, and tenderness
exam.meaning: Thyroid disease is common in women and explains menstrual irregularity, weight change, and mood symptoms that overlap with perimenopause and depression. A goiter or nodule triggers a TSH and, for nodules, an ultrasound; treating thyroid disease often resolves the menstrual complaint that brought her in.

exam.maneuver: Perform a clinical breast exam, including the axilla and supraclavicular area
exam.meaning: The exam evaluates symptoms she reports and complements — never replaces — mammography. A dominant mass or spontaneous discharge triggers diagnostic mammogram with targeted ultrasound, not routine screening. Document quadrant, size, and mobility so the finding can be tracked.

exam.maneuver: Inspect the external genitalia, including the vulva, introitus, and perineum
exam.meaning: Condyloma, herpes lesions, Bartholin cysts, and lichen sclerosus are all visible here and often missed if you go straight to the speculum. A suspicious vulvar lesion gets biopsied; warts get treated with counseling about HPV; whitened atrophic patches suggest lichen sclerosus, which needs biopsy and potent topical steroids given the malignancy risk.

exam.maneuver: Perform a speculum exam to visualize the cervix, vaginal walls, and any discharge or bleeding
exam.meaning: Direct visualization locates discharge and bleeding and spots cervical lesions a Pap alone would miss. A pelvic exam is not required for starting or refilling contraception — do the speculum exam when screening is due or symptoms warrant it. A friable or visibly abnormal cervix gets biopsied or referred for colposcopy; purulent discharge gets NAAT testing and treatment.

exam.maneuver: Collect cervical screening — cytology, HPV testing, or co-testing — when due by age and history
exam.meaning: This is the test that prevents cervical cancer by catching HPV infection and precancer early. Collect per the age-based schedule — cytology every 3 years at 21 to 29, co-testing every 5 years or primary HPV at 30 to 65. Abnormal results get triaged per ASCCP guidance, with colposcopy for high-grade findings.

exam.maneuver: Perform a bimanual exam to assess uterine size, shape, mobility, and the adnexae
exam.meaning: Bimanual exam detects fibroids, adenomyosis, ovarian masses, and pelvic inflammatory disease that history alone misses. An enlarged irregular uterus triggers a pelvic ultrasound; an adnexal mass triggers ultrasound with tumor markers guided by age and menopause status; cervical motion tenderness triggers PID evaluation and treatment.

exam.maneuver: Perform a rectovaginal exam when indicated — posterior pelvic pain, suspected endometriosis, or abnormal bleeding
exam.meaning: The rectovaginal exam reaches the posterior cul-de-sac and uterosacral ligaments where endometriosis implants hide. Nodularity or tenderness there points to endometriosis and changes management toward hormonal suppression or surgical evaluation. A rectal mass redirects to colorectal workup.

exam.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for masses, tenderness, and organ enlargement
exam.meaning: A fibroid uterus or ovarian mass large enough to feel abdominally changes the urgency of imaging. A palpable mass triggers a pelvic ultrasound to characterize it; combined with bimanual findings it helps distinguish uterine from adnexal origin.

exam.maneuver: Inspect skin and hair for hirsutism, acne, acanthosis nigricans, and androgenic alopecia
exam.meaning: Hirsutism with irregular menses points to PCOS, which carries metabolic and endometrial risk; acanthosis nigricans signals insulin resistance. These findings trigger an androgen and glucose workup and diabetes screening rather than cosmetic dismissal. Persistent anovulation from PCOS also needs endometrial protection.

exam.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and lungs
exam.meaning: A baseline cardiopulmonary exam matters before prescribing estrogen-containing contraception and catches murmurs or reactive airway disease worth addressing. A pathologic-sounding murmur triggers an echocardiogram; uncontrolled hypertension found here steers contraception toward progestin-only or non-hormonal methods.

exam.maneuver: Assess gait, mobility, and fall risk in older patients
exam.meaning: Falls are a major source of morbidity after menopause, and bone loss accelerates in the same years. An unsteady gait triggers physical therapy referral, home safety counseling, and vitamin D and bone density assessment. It also informs whether hormone therapy discussions should weigh fracture risk.

history.question: How did you find out you're pregnant, and how are you feeling about this pregnancy?
history.meaning: The discovery story anchors dating — the date of a positive home test sets the earliest confirmed gestational age — and her feelings screen for ambivalence or distress. If she is unsure about continuing, pivot to nondirective options counseling and timely referral, since gestational age limits options. Enthusiasm or anxiety both open the door to discussing support systems.

history.question: What was the first day of your last menstrual period, and are your cycles regular?
history.meaning: Naegele's rule — add 7 days and subtract 3 months from the LMP — gives the estimated due date, but only when cycles are regular and the LMP is certain. Irregular cycles or an uncertain LMP make the LMP-based date unreliable. In that case, a first-trimester ultrasound becomes the dating standard, since it is the most accurate dating method available.

history.question: Have you had an ultrasound yet in this pregnancy? Was this pregnancy conceived with fertility treatment?
history.meaning: An early ultrasound confirms viability, number of fetuses, and dates; IVF transfer dates give exact dating that overrides the LMP. Multiple gestation discovered here changes everything — referral to high-risk care with earlier anatomy and growth scans. If no scan exists and dating is uncertain, order a dating ultrasound now, and outline the road ahead: anatomy ultrasound at 18 to 22 weeks and glucose screening at 24 to 28 weeks.

history.question: Have you had any vaginal bleeding, cramping, severe nausea and vomiting, headaches, vision changes, or swelling?
history.meaning: Bleeding with cramping raises ectopic pregnancy and threatened or spontaneous abortion; severe vomiting suggests hyperemesis gravidarum; headache with vision changes suggests preeclampsia once past 20 weeks. Bleeding or pain triggers quantitative hCG and ultrasound; hyperemesis triggers labs, fluids, and antiemetics; headache with hypertension triggers a preeclampsia workup.

history.question: Tell me about each prior pregnancy — how far along you were, and whether it ended in a vaginal birth, C-section, miscarriage, or termination.
history.meaning: The GTPAL history predicts labor course and flags risk: grand multiparity raises postpartum hemorrhage risk, and prior losses shape counseling and surveillance. Document each pregnancy's outcome and gestational age. Prior term vaginal deliveries are reassuring for labor progress; a history of loss may warrant earlier ultrasound and closer follow-up.

history.question: With prior pregnancies, did you have high blood pressure or preeclampsia, preterm birth, gestational diabetes, heavy bleeding, or a stillbirth?
history.meaning: Obstetric complications recur: prior preeclampsia, prior spontaneous preterm birth, prior gestational diabetes, and prior stillbirth each raise the risk in this pregnancy. The answers drive concrete prevention — low-dose aspirin starting between 12 and 28 weeks after prior preeclampsia, progesterone plus serial cervical length after prior spontaneous preterm birth, early glucose screening after prior gestational diabetes, and antenatal surveillance after stillbirth.

history.question: Have you had a C-section or any surgery on your uterus? If so, how many, what kind of incision, and why?
history.meaning: The uterine scar determines delivery planning and rupture risk: a prior low transverse incision may allow a trial of labor, while a classical incision or a myomectomy entering the cavity mandates a scheduled repeat C-section. Get the operative report rather than trusting memory. Multiple prior C-sections raise placenta accreta risk and warrant early placental location imaging.

history.question: Do you have high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid disease, asthma, seizures, depression, or any heart condition?
history.meaning: Chronic hypertension, pregestational diabetes, thyroid disease, epilepsy, and psychiatric illness all change prenatal care from routine to co-managed. Chronic hypertension triggers aspirin prophylaxis and growth scans; diabetes demands tight glycemic control and early anatomy screening; hypothyroidism needs prompt levothyroxine adjustment for fetal brain development; psychiatric medications get a risk-benefit review with continuation of effective treatment.

history.question: Have you had any surgeries — especially abdominal, pelvic, or spine surgery?
history.meaning: Prior abdominal or pelvic surgery hints at adhesions that matter for C-section planning, and spine surgery or hardware affects neuraxial anesthesia options. A lumbar fusion or spinal hardware triggers an anesthesia consult well before labor. Document scars on exam to match the history.

history.question: What medications, vitamins, and supplements do you take — prescription, over-the-counter, and herbal?
history.meaning: The first trimester is organogenesis, when teratogens do their damage: ACE inhibitors, valproate, isotretinoin, and methotrexate must be stopped and replaced. Review every product against teratogen resources rather than assuming safety. Continue folic acid and switch essential medications to pregnancy-compatible alternatives instead of stopping treatment outright.

history.question: Do you have any drug allergies, and what happens when you take them?
history.meaning: Allergy history determines antibiotic choices for group B strep prophylaxis in labor and for any intrapartum infection. A true penicillin allergy changes the GBS prophylaxis plan to clindamycin or vancomycin per susceptibility. Document reaction type now so labor orders are safe.

history.question: Have you ever had HIV, syphilis, gonorrhea, chlamydia, herpes, hepatitis B or C, or chickenpox? Do you know if you're immune to rubella?
history.meaning: Vertical transmission makes these infections pregnancy problems, not just personal ones: HIV needs antiretrovirals and delivery planning, syphilis needs penicillin treatment to prevent congenital syphilis, hepatitis B triggers neonatal immunoprophylaxis. Non-immunity to rubella or varicella means vaccinating postpartum. Order the standard panel today — CBC, blood type and antibody screen, rubella immunity, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B — plus chlamydia and gonorrhea NAAT.

history.question: Have you thought about genetic screening — like cell-free DNA testing, carrier screening, or first-trimester screening? These are all optional.
history.meaning: Cell-free DNA, carrier screening for conditions like cystic fibrosis and spinal muscular atrophy, and first-trimester screening are time-sensitive and entirely optional — counseling must be nondirective. Advanced maternal age and family history raise aneuploidy risk and may prompt genetics referral. Order what she chooses after informed consent, and document declinations.

history.question: Do you smoke or vape, drink alcohol, or use marijuana or other drugs?
history.meaning: Tobacco raises preterm birth and growth restriction risk, alcohol can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders with no known safe amount, and drug use affects neonatal planning. Pregnancy is a powerful motivator — offer quitline and counseling referrals now. Opioid use triggers referral to treatment and planning for neonatal abstinence monitoring rather than judgment.

history.question: Are you taking folic acid or a prenatal vitamin? What does a typical day of eating look like, and how has your weight changed?
history.meaning: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects and works only if started early — ideally before conception. Pre-pregnancy BMI sets the weight-gain target, and poor intake or severe vomiting flags nutritional risk. Start or continue folic acid, counsel on weight-gain goals and food safety like avoiding raw fish and unpasteurized cheese, and evaluate persistent weight loss.

history.question: Do you feel safe at home? Any chemical, radiation, or heavy-lifting exposures at work? Are your flu, COVID, and Tdap vaccines current?
listenFor: work in a lab with solvents
history.meaning: Intimate partner violence can escalate in pregnancy, workplace teratogens need occupational health review, and vaccines protect both mother and newborn — influenza and COVID are safe in pregnancy and Tdap is given with each pregnancy at 27 to 36 weeks to protect the infant from pertussis. A safety concern triggers private assessment and resources; exposures trigger occupational referral; missing flu and COVID vaccines get given today while Tdap is timed for the third trimester.

exam.maneuver: Record blood pressure, heart rate, weight, and BMI
exam.meaning: Baseline blood pressure is the reference that later distinguishes chronic hypertension from preeclampsia — without it, a mid-pregnancy elevation cannot be interpreted. Elevated baseline pressure triggers evaluation for chronic hypertension and aspirin prophylaxis. Baseline BMI sets the weight-gain target and flags gestational diabetes risk.

exam.maneuver: Palpate the thyroid
exam.meaning: Maternal hypothyroidism impairs fetal neurodevelopment, and pregnancy increases thyroid hormone demand. A goiter or nodule triggers a TSH check. Overt hypothyroidism gets treated promptly with levothyroxine dose adjustment.

exam.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and lungs
exam.meaning: Pregnancy expands blood volume and cardiac output, so baseline cardiac disease must be known before that load arrives. A pathologic-sounding murmur triggers an echocardiogram; wheezing triggers asthma optimization, since uncontrolled asthma raises preterm birth risk.

exam.maneuver: Examine the breasts
exam.meaning: A baseline breast exam catches dominant masses, which still need diagnostic workup in pregnancy with pregnancy-safe imaging. Flat or inverted nipples are not a contraindication to breastfeeding but prompt early lactation support planning.

exam.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for masses, tenderness, and surgical scars
exam.meaning: Fibroids and adnexal masses found now get characterized by ultrasound and followed, since they can complicate pregnancy. Documenting scars corroborates the surgical history for delivery planning.

exam.maneuver: Check for lower extremity edema
exam.meaning: Baseline edema status matters because new or worsening edema with hypertension later suggests preeclampsia. Marked edema this early with elevated pressure triggers a preeclampsia workup; physiologic trace edema gets reassurance.

exam.maneuver: Inspect the external genitalia
exam.meaning: Genital lesions change delivery planning: active herpes lesions at term mean C-section to prevent neonatal herpes, and bulky obstructing condyloma may also require C-section. Document lesions now and counsel on suppression therapy later in pregnancy if herpes is recurrent.

exam.maneuver: Perform a speculum exam — assess the cervix and discharge, and collect a Pap if due
exam.meaning: Pregnancy does not change cervical screening — if she is due, collect it now. Discharge gets NAAT testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea, which are treated in pregnancy to prevent preterm rupture and neonatal infection. Note cervical appearance as a baseline.

exam.maneuver: Perform a bimanual exam to assess uterine size versus dates and palpate the adnexae
exam.meaning: Uterine size corroborates dating: a size-date mismatch points to wrong dates, fibroids, or multiple gestation and triggers a dating ultrasound. An adnexal mass gets ultrasound characterization and surveillance, since most are benign corpus luteum cysts.

exam.maneuver: Check fetal heart tones with Doppler if gestational age is 10 to 12 weeks or more
exam.meaning: Audible tones confirm viability and reassure, but absence before 10 to 12 weeks is normal and should not alarm. If tones are absent when expected by dates, get an ultrasound rather than repeating blindly.

exam.maneuver: Check deep tendon reflexes as a baseline
exam.meaning: Hyperreflexia and clonus are neurologic signs of preeclampsia, but they are uninterpretable without a baseline. Document reflexes now; new hyperreflexia later with hypertension triggers a preeclampsia evaluation and magnesium planning.

exam.maneuver: Inspect the skin
exam.meaning: Chloasma and linea nigra are normal pigment changes of pregnancy worth naming so she does not worry. Severe pruritus, especially on palms and soles, suggests intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy and triggers bile acid testing, since it raises stillbirth risk.

history.question: Tell me about the bleeding — when did your normal pattern change, and what changed?
history.meaning: Onset and tempo separate acute emergencies from chronic problems and point into the PALM-COEIN framework — structural causes like polyps, adenomyosis, and fibroids versus non-structural causes like coagulopathy, ovulatory dysfunction, endometrial disorders, and medications. Sudden severe bleeding triggers urgent stabilization; a gradual change allows an outpatient workup.

history.question: How often do your periods come, and are they regular and predictable?
history.meaning: Regular predictable cycles suggest ovulatory bleeding, which points toward structural causes — polyps, adenomyosis, leiomyoma — while irregular unpredictable bleeding points to ovulatory dysfunction from PCOS, thyroid disease, or perimenopause. Regular heavy bleeding triggers a pelvic ultrasound first; irregular bleeding adds TSH, prolactin, and androgen evaluation.

history.question: How many days does the bleeding last?
history.meaning: Prolonged bleeding raises anemia risk and suggests anovulatory cycles, submucosal fibroids, or polyps rather than normal menses. Bleeding beyond 7 days triggers a CBC and ferritin plus imaging; continuous prolonged bleeding may need urgent hormonal control.

history.question: On your heaviest day, how many pads or tampons do you use, and do you pass clots or flood through clothes or bedding?
history.meaning: Volume quantifies severity: soaking through hourly, passing large clots, or flooding signals heavy menstrual bleeding that causes iron deficiency and disrupts life. Severe volume triggers a CBC, iron studies, and consideration of urgent evaluation; it also steers treatment toward potent options like tranexamic acid or hormonal therapy rather than watchful waiting.

history.question: Does the bleeding keep you from work, school, or activities? Do you feel tired, dizzy, short of breath, or notice a racing heart?
history.meaning: Functional impact is what makes bleeding worth treating aggressively, and dizziness, dyspnea, or palpitations signal significant anemia. Symptomatic anemia triggers a stat CBC, iron repletion, and urgent bleeding control — sometimes in the emergency department. The impact also guides shared decision-making between medical and procedural options.

history.question: Do you bleed between periods, or bleed after sex?
history.meaning: Intermenstrual bleeding points to endometrial polyps, hyperplasia, or submucosal fibroids; postcoital bleeding points to the cervix — polyps, cervicitis, or cervical cancer. Either finding triggers a speculum exam to localize the source, a pelvic ultrasound, and confirmation that cervical screening is current, with endometrial sampling when risk factors stack up.

history.question: When was your last period, and is there any chance you could be pregnant?
listenFor: could be — we don't use contraception
history.meaning: A pregnancy test comes before everything in abnormal bleeding: ectopic pregnancy and threatened or spontaneous abortion both bleed and both change management completely. A positive test triggers quantitative hCG and ultrasound and rules out hormonal bleeding treatments. Never start tranexamic acid or hormones for bleeding until pregnancy is excluded.

history.question: Are your periods becoming irregular or stopping — and have you had any bleeding after going 12 months without a period?
listenFor: bleeding after a year without periods
history.meaning: Perimenopause brings anovulatory bleeding that is usually benign but overlaps with the age when endometrial cancer risk rises. Any postmenopausal bleeding is endometrial cancer until proven otherwise. Postmenopausal bleeding triggers endometrial sampling plus transvaginal ultrasound without delay; persistent perimenopausal bleeding lowers the threshold for sampling too.

history.question: Do you have pelvic pain, severe cramps, pressure or a feeling of fullness, or pain with sex?
history.meaning: Severe dysmenorrhea suggests adenomyosis or endometriosis, bulk and pressure symptoms suggest fibroids, and dyspareunia fits endometriosis or adenomyosis. These symptoms steer imaging: bulk symptoms trigger a pelvic ultrasound to map fibroids, and suspected adenomyosis or endometriosis changes treatment toward hormonal suppression.

history.question: Have you noticed excess facial or body hair, acne, weight gain, milky nipple discharge, or feeling unusually hot or cold?
history.meaning: Hirsutism and acne with irregular bleeding point to PCOS; galactorrhea points to hyperprolactinemia; cold intolerance and fatigue point to hypothyroidism — all ovulatory dysfunction causes in the COEIN half. Hirsutism triggers androgen and glucose evaluation, galactorrhea triggers a prolactin level, and thyroid symptoms trigger a TSH; treating the endocrine cause often normalizes bleeding.

history.question: Do you bruise easily, get frequent nosebleeds or bleeding gums, or bleed heavily after cuts, dental work, or childbirth? Anyone in your family with a bleeding disorder?
history.meaning: Bleeding elsewhere in the body suggests an inherited or acquired coagulopathy — von Willebrand disease is the classic culprit in heavy menstrual bleeding — rather than a uterine problem. A positive screen triggers von Willebrand factor testing and hematology referral, and it changes treatment toward tranexamic acid or desmopressin rather than surgery.

history.question: How many pregnancies have you had, and have you had any C-sections?
history.meaning: Nulliparity raises endometrial hyperplasia and cancer risk through unopposed estrogen exposure, while prior C-sections raise the possibility of an isthmocele — a scar defect that causes postmenstrual spotting. Risk factors from this history lower the threshold for endometrial sampling and shape ultrasound interpretation.

history.question: What medications do you take — especially blood thinners, aspirin, hormonal birth control, or an IUD? Have you used tamoxifen?
history.meaning: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets, hormonal contraception, copper IUDs, and tamoxifen are all iatrogenic causes of bleeding — the I in PALM-COEIN. A copper IUD with heavy bleeding suggests switching to a hormonal IUD; anticoagulant-related bleeding needs coordination with the prescribing clinician; tamoxifen mandates endometrial evaluation given its cancer risk.

history.question: Any drug allergies? Do you smoke or drink alcohol?
listenFor: smoke half a pack a day
history.meaning: Allergies must be documented before prescribing tranexamic acid or hormonal therapy. Smoking adds cardiovascular risk that matters when considering estrogen-containing treatments. Neither changes the diagnosis, but both constrain which bleeding treatments are safe to offer.

exam.maneuver: Record vital signs, including orthostatics if bleeding is heavy
exam.meaning: Tachycardia, hypotension, or orthostatic changes signal hemodynamically significant blood loss that cannot wait for an outpatient workup. Instability triggers emergency department transfer, IV fluids, and transfusion consideration. Stable vitals allow a clinic-based workup.

exam.maneuver: Inspect for pallor of the conjunctivae, nail beds, and palms
exam.meaning: Pallor is the bedside clue to anemia when labs are not yet back. Visible pallor triggers a stat CBC and iron studies and raises the urgency of bleeding control. Absence of pallor does not rule out iron deficiency, but it lowers the acuity.

exam.maneuver: Palpate the thyroid
exam.meaning: Thyroid disease is a reversible non-structural cause of abnormal bleeding in the COEIN group. A goiter or nodule triggers a TSH; treating hypo- or hyperthyroidism often normalizes the bleeding without any gynecologic procedure.

exam.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen for an enlarged uterus, masses, or tenderness
exam.meaning: A fibroid uterus large enough to feel abdominally explains heavy bleeding and bulk symptoms and sets the scale of disease. A palpable mass triggers a pelvic ultrasound to map fibroids or characterize an adnexal mass, and size guides whether medical therapy is plausible or surgery is likely.

exam.maneuver: Inspect the external genitalia for lesions, trauma, or active bleeding
exam.meaning: The source of bleeding must be localized before assuming it is uterine — vulvar lesions, trauma, and vaginal sources all present as vaginal bleeding. A vulvar lesion gets biopsied; confirmed vaginal origin redirects the workup away from the uterus.

exam.maneuver: Perform a speculum exam to identify the bleeding source — cervical, vaginal, or uterine
exam.meaning: This is the key maneuver: blood coming through the cervical os means a uterine source, while a cervical lesion means the cervix itself. A cervical polyp can be removed in clinic; a friable mass gets biopsied urgently for suspected cervical cancer; blood from the os with a normal cervix sends the workup to pelvic ultrasound.

exam.maneuver: Perform a bimanual exam for uterine size, contour, mobility, and adnexal masses
exam.meaning: An enlarged irregular uterus suggests fibroids, a boggy tender uterus suggests adenomyosis, and an adnexal mass raises ovarian pathology. Findings trigger a pelvic ultrasound; a fixed irregular mass raises malignancy concern and accelerates the workup. Cervical motion tenderness would redirect toward pelvic inflammatory disease.

exam.maneuver: Perform a rectovaginal exam when posterior disease is suspected
exam.meaning: The rectovaginal exam reaches the posterior cul-de-sac where endometriosis implants cause bleeding-associated pain. Nodularity points to endometriosis and steers treatment toward hormonal suppression or surgical evaluation rather than endometrial ablation alone.

exam.maneuver: Examine the skin for petechiae, purpura, and ecchymoses
exam.meaning: Petechiae and easy bruising point to platelet or coagulation disorders — the coagulopathy arm of PALM-COEIN — rather than a uterine cause. Abnormal findings trigger a CBC with platelets, coagulation studies, and hematology referral, and they argue against procedural management until the bleeding disorder is addressed.

exam.maneuver: Examine the breasts and check for galactorrhea
exam.meaning: Galactorrhea signals hyperprolactinemia, which causes anovulation and abnormal bleeding. Expressible milky discharge triggers a prolactin level and medication review, with brain imaging if prolactin is markedly elevated; treating the prolactin excess often restores ovulation and normal bleeding.

history.question: When did the discharge start, and has it changed since then?
history.meaning: The timeline separates an acute new infection from something recurrent or chronic. A new discharge after a new partner points toward trichomoniasis or cervicitis from chlamydia or gonorrhea, while a discharge that keeps returning after treatment points toward recurrent bacterial vaginosis or candidiasis. If it started right after a course of antibiotics, candida moves to the top; if it never fully cleared, plan to re-examine and test rather than repeating the same prescription.

history.question: What color is the discharge?
history.meaning: Color narrows the differential before you even look. Thin gray-white discharge is classic for bacterial vaginosis; thick white clumpy discharge points to candidiasis; frothy yellow-green discharge is classic for trichomoniasis. A purulent yellow discharge coming from the cervix instead points to cervicitis from chlamydia or gonorrhea, which changes the workup to NAAT testing and the treatment to ceftriaxone plus doxycycline.

history.question: What does it look like — thin and watery, thick and clumpy, or bubbly and frothy?
history.meaning: Consistency backs up what the color suggests and separates vaginal causes from cervical ones. Thick cottage-cheese discharge clinging to the vaginal walls is classic for candidiasis and gets an antifungal; thin homogeneous discharge coating the walls is classic for BV and gets metronidazole. Frothy discharge points to trichomoniasis, which needs metronidazole plus partner treatment — a different plan than either of the other two.

history.question: Is there an odor? What does it smell like?
history.meaning: A fishy odor is the hallmark of bacterial vaginosis, caused by anaerobic overgrowth producing amines, and you can confirm it on exam with the whiff test. A foul or strong odor with yellow-green discharge points toward trichomoniasis. Little to no odor with thick white discharge fits candidiasis. A fishy odor history lets you counsel the patient on the likely diagnosis and plan a wet mount to look for clue cells before prescribing metronidazole.

history.question: Do you have itching or burning around the vulva or vagina?
history.meaning: Itching is the symptom that most strongly separates candida from BV and trich — prominent vulvovaginal itching with thick white discharge is classic for candidiasis. Burning, especially of the vulva, also fits candida, while BV usually causes little itching. If itching dominates, plan for antifungal treatment and counsel against scratching, which worsens excoriations; if there is no itching at all, lean away from candida.

history.question: Does it burn when you urinate, or hurt with sex?
history.meaning: Pain with urination or sex tells you the inflammation involves the vulva, urethra, or cervix, not just the vagina. External dysuria — burning as urine hits the vulva — fits candidal vulvitis; deep dyspareunia with discharge points toward cervicitis or pelvic inflammatory disease. Dyspareunia with postcoital bleeding should trigger chlamydia and gonorrhea testing, because cervicitis needs ceftriaxone plus doxycycline and partner therapy, not just a vaginal prescription.

history.question: Any bleeding after sex, or bleeding between periods?
history.meaning: Bleeding after sex is a red flag for cervicitis — an inflamed, friable cervix bleeds on contact, most often from chlamydia or gonorrhea. It also raises concern for a cervical lesion, so it changes the exam: you need a careful speculum look at the cervix itself, not just the discharge. Finding cervical friability means NAAT testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea and empiric treatment while results are pending.

history.question: Are you sexually active? Have you had any new partners in the last couple of months?
history.meaning: Trichomoniasis and cervicitis from chlamydia or gonorrhea are sexually transmitted, so new or multiple partners raise their probability directly. BV is not classified as an STI but is strongly associated with new sexual partners and unprotected sex. A new partner with frothy or purulent discharge means test for STIs and treat partners; with a long-term monogamous partner and no new exposures, recurrent BV or candida are more likely and partner treatment is not needed.

history.question: Do you use condoms? Every time?
history.meaning: Consistent condom use lowers the risk of trichomoniasis, chlamydia, and gonorrhea, so inconsistent use keeps those on the table. For recurrent BV, counseling on consistent condom use is part of prevention since semen raises vaginal pH and disrupts flora. If condoms are used consistently and correctly, an STI cause is less likely and you can focus on BV or candida.

history.question: Do you douche, or have you started any new soaps, laundry detergent, or feminine products?
history.meaning: Douching disrupts normal lactobacillus flora and is a well-known risk factor for bacterial vaginosis — stopping douching is part of treatment and prevention, so this question directly changes counseling. New soaps, scented products, or detergents can cause contact irritation that mimics infectious discharge with itching and burning. If the story is new products plus irritation without classic infectious features, removing the irritant may be the whole treatment.

history.question: When was your last period? Is there any chance you could be pregnant?
history.meaning: Pregnancy changes drug choices: oral fluconazole is avoided in pregnancy, so candida gets topical azoles instead, while BV and trichomoniasis are still treated. A missed period with discharge also forces you to consider pregnancy-related causes if pain or bleeding coexist. Get a urine pregnancy test on every patient with a new discharge complaint and document the last menstrual period before prescribing anything.

history.question: Have you had discharge like this before? What was it called, and what treated it?
history.meaning: Recurrent episodes with the same treatment response define the pattern — recurrent BV or recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis have specific management with longer or suppressive regimens rather than another single dose. Knowing what worked before guides empiric choice when the presentation matches, and knowing what failed tells you to test rather than repeat. Ask what the prior diagnosis was called and what drug was given, since patients often misremember names.

history.question: Any fever, chills, or lower belly pain along with the discharge?
history.meaning: Fever or lower abdominal pain with discharge moves you from vaginitis to pelvic inflammatory disease, which is a different disease with different stakes — PID can cause infertility and ectopic pregnancy. Discharge plus cervical motion tenderness or fever meets criteria to treat for PID with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline rather than a vaginal-only regimen. If fever is present, also consider tubo-ovarian abscess and whether she needs inpatient care instead of a clinic prescription.

history.question: Are you on any medications, especially antibiotics or birth control? Any drug allergies?
history.meaning: Recent antibiotics commonly trigger candidiasis by wiping out lactobacilli, so discharge starting after antibiotics is candida until proven otherwise. Combined hormonal contraception can increase candidiasis risk. Allergies matter directly: a metronidazole allergy changes BV and trich treatment options, and anyone getting metronidazole needs counseling to avoid alcohol during treatment and after.

exam.maneuver: Vital signs: temperature, blood pressure, heart rate
exam.meaning: Fever with discharge suggests pelvic inflammatory disease or tubo-ovarian abscess rather than simple vaginitis. Tachycardia or hypotension are late signs of sepsis from a pelvic source and change the disposition to emergent evaluation. Normal vitals with isolated discharge keep you in the outpatient vaginitis pathway.

exam.maneuver: Abdominal exam: palpate for lower abdominal tenderness, rebound, guarding
exam.meaning: Lower abdominal tenderness with discharge supports PID; rebound or guarding raises concern for peritonitis from a ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess. A soft, nontender abdomen with isolated vaginal symptoms keeps the differential in vaginitis and cervicitis. Marked tenderness changes management to PID treatment and consideration of imaging or admission.

exam.maneuver: External genital exam: inspect vulva for erythema, edema, excoriations, fissures, ulcers, or vesicles
exam.meaning: Look for vulvar erythema, edema, and excoriations — classic for candidal vulvovaginitis — and for ulcers or vesicles that would point to herpes instead. Fissures and excoriations also tell you how much itching the patient has endured. Finding herpetic lesions changes the plan entirely to HSV testing and antivirals, not antifungals.

exam.maneuver: Speculum exam: visualize the vaginal walls and cervix; characterize discharge color, consistency, amount, odor, and whether it comes from the cervical os or the vaginal walls
exam.meaning: Seeing the discharge yourself confirms the history: thin gray-white coating the walls means BV, thick white curds mean candida, frothy yellow-green means trich, and purulent discharge from the cervical os means cervicitis. Discharge from the os versus the walls is the key distinction — endocervical pus means chlamydia and gonorrhea testing and different antibiotics. Document color, consistency, amount, and odor in your own words.

exam.maneuver: Vaginal pH testing with pH paper on the lateral vaginal wall (avoid cervical mucus)
exam.meaning: A pH above 4.5 supports BV or trichomoniasis; a normal pH of 4.5 or below supports candidiasis, since yeast thrives in normal acidic pH. pH is a fast bedside test that narrows the differential before the wet mount is even read. An elevated pH with a positive whiff test is classic for BV and supports empiric metronidazole.

exam.maneuver: Whiff (KOH) test: add potassium hydroxide to discharge on a slide and smell for fishy amine odor
findings: KOH reveals yeast forms on microscopy
exam.meaning: Adding KOH to discharge releases a fishy amine odor in bacterial vaginosis — a positive whiff test is one of the bedside criteria for BV. A negative whiff test with thick discharge points away from BV toward candida. KOH also dissolves cellular material so yeast forms become visible on the same slide, making this one step do double duty.

exam.maneuver: Wet mount microscopy: saline prep examined for clue cells, hyphae/pseudohyphae, and motile trichomonads
exam.meaning: Microscopy gives you the diagnosis at the bedside: clue cells (epithelial cells studded with bacteria) mean BV, hyphae or pseudohyphae mean candida, motile trichomonads mean trichomoniasis. Seeing the organism lets you treat confidently the same visit instead of waiting on cultures. No organisms with persistent symptoms means reconsidering — re-examine the cervix and send NAATs for chlamydia and gonorrhea.

exam.maneuver: Cervical assessment on speculum: look for endocervical discharge and touch the cervix to check for friability (bleeds easily)
exam.meaning: Endocervical discharge or a cervix that bleeds when touched means cervicitis until proven otherwise — most often chlamydia or gonorrhea. This finding changes the plan from vaginal treatment to NAAT testing plus empiric ceftriaxone and doxycycline with partner therapy. A normal, non-friable cervix keeps you in the vaginitis pathway.

exam.maneuver: Bimanual exam: assess for cervical motion tenderness, uterine tenderness, and adnexal tenderness or masses
exam.meaning: Cervical motion tenderness or uterine and adnexal tenderness with discharge meets clinical criteria for PID and mandates PID treatment, not just vaginitis therapy. An adnexal mass with fever suggests tubo-ovarian abscess, which may need admission and imaging. A nontender exam keeps management outpatient and focused on the vaginal diagnosis.

exam.maneuver: Urine pregnancy test
exam.meaning: A positive test changes drug choices — avoid oral fluconazole in pregnancy and use topical azoles for candida — and changes counseling for BV and trich, which are still treated in pregnancy. It also forces you to consider pregnancy-related causes if pain or bleeding coexist. Get it before prescribing, not after.

history.question: When did the pain start — suddenly out of nowhere, or gradually?
history.meaning: Sudden severe pain is the pattern of surgical emergencies — ovarian torsion and ruptured ectopic — while gradual or chronic pain points toward PID, endometriosis, or fibroids. The tempo of onset is the fastest way to sort 'go to the OR now' from 'work up as an outpatient.' If the pain started abruptly and is severe, move fast: pregnancy test, vitals, and ultrasound without delay.

history.question: Where exactly is the pain, and does it move or spread anywhere?
history.meaning: Unilateral pain points to an ovarian source — torsion, corpus luteum cyst, or tubo-ovarian abscess — while diffuse bilateral lower abdominal pain with discharge points to PID. Pain radiating to the shoulder suggests diaphragmatic irritation from blood in the abdomen, a classic clue for ruptured ectopic. Localizing the pain focuses the ultrasound on the right structures and tells you which emergency to rule out first.

history.question: How would you describe it — sharp, dull, crampy, stabbing?
history.meaning: Sharp, stabbing pain fits torsion or a ruptured cyst; dull, aching, constant pain fits PID or endometriosis; crampy pain with bleeding fits miscarriage or dysmenorrhea. Character alone never makes the diagnosis, but it weights the differential before you examine. Colicky pain that comes in waves is unusual for gynecologic causes and should make you consider a ureteral stone or bowel problem instead.

history.question: How bad is it on a scale of 1 to 10, and is it getting worse?
history.meaning: The number matters less than the trajectory and function — pain that is worsening or keeping her from standing or walking signals an acute process that needs urgent evaluation. Severe pain with a positive pregnancy test and bleeding is ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise. Documenting severity also gives you a baseline to judge whether treatment is working.

history.question: Does the pain come and go with your periods, or is it there all the time?
history.meaning: Pain that starts with menses and eases after is dysmenorrhea; when it is severe, progressive, and paired with deep dyspareunia or painful bowel movements, think endometriosis. A bulky, tender uterus with heavy painful periods points to adenomyosis; a uniformly enlarged uterus with bulk symptoms points to fibroids. Cyclic pain changes management toward hormonal suppression and an endometriosis workup rather than an acute surgical evaluation.

history.question: When was your last period? Is there any chance you could be pregnant?
history.meaning: Every pelvic pain workup starts with whether she could be pregnant — a positive test with pain and bleeding is ectopic until proven otherwise, and that is the can't-miss diagnosis. The last menstrual period dates the pregnancy and tells you what a quantitative hCG and ultrasound should show. If she could be pregnant, get the urine pregnancy test before anything else, and never let a reassuring history substitute for the test.

history.question: Any vaginal bleeding — spotting, or heavier than normal?
history.meaning: Bleeding with pain and a positive pregnancy test raises ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage; heavy bleeding with clots and cramping in early pregnancy points to miscarriage. Bleeding between periods with chronic pain points toward fibroids, polyps, or anovulation rather than an emergency. The bleeding pattern decides whether you need a quantitative hCG with serial monitoring or a pelvic ultrasound looking for structural causes.

history.question: Any dizziness, lightheadedness, or feeling like you might faint?
history.meaning: Fainting, near-fainting, or dizziness with pelvic pain and bleeding means she is losing blood — ruptured ectopic with blood in the abdomen is the classic cause. This is a resuscitation situation, not a clinic workup: type and screen, large-bore IV access, and emergent OB/GYN involvement. Even without frank syncope, orthostatic symptoms with a positive pregnancy test should be treated as unstable until proven otherwise.

history.question: Any fever, chills, or vaginal discharge with the pain?
history.meaning: Fever with pelvic pain points to infection — PID or tubo-ovarian abscess — especially with vaginal discharge or recent new sexual partners. Fever plus a tender adnexal mass is tubo-ovarian abscess until proven otherwise, which may need admission and IV antibiotics. No fever with chronic cyclic pain points away from infection and toward endometriosis.

history.question: Does it hurt with sex? Any pain with bowel movements or when you pee?
listenFor: hurts to poop on my period
history.meaning: Deep dyspareunia — pain with deep penetration — is classic for endometriosis, as is pain with bowel movements during menses when implants involve the rectum. Dysuria with frequency points to a urinary cause like cystitis rather than a gynecologic one. These associated symptoms map the pain to adjacent organs and decide whether the workup stays gynecologic or expands to urology or GI.

history.question: Have you ever had a sexually transmitted infection or pelvic inflammatory disease?
history.meaning: A history of chlamydia, gonorrhea, or PID markedly raises the risk of recurrent PID and of tubal damage that predisposes to ectopic pregnancy. It raises the pretest probability that current pain with discharge is PID again. With this history, have a lower threshold to treat empirically for PID and to counsel about infertility and ectopic risk going forward.

history.question: Any prior abdominal or pelvic surgeries? Have you been told you have endometriosis?
history.meaning: Prior pelvic surgery raises the risk of adhesions, a common cause of chronic pelvic pain, and known endometriosis makes recurrence the leading diagnosis for new cyclic pain. A history of ectopic pregnancy or tubal surgery raises the risk of another ectopic. This history changes the workup: known endometriosis with classic symptoms may not need repeat laparoscopy before starting hormonal suppression.

history.question: What have you taken for the pain, and did it help? Any drug allergies?
history.meaning: What she has tried and what helped guides next steps — pain relieved by NSAIDs fits dysmenorrhea and supports continuing them, while pain unresponsive to NSAIDs raises concern for torsion or another surgical cause. It also keeps you from prescribing something she already failed. Document allergies here too, since an NSAID allergy changes the dysmenorrhea plan.

history.question: Have you ever been pregnant — any deliveries, miscarriages, or ectopic pregnancies?
history.meaning: Prior pregnancies, miscarriages, and especially prior ectopics directly change risk — a prior ectopic is one of the strongest risk factors for another. Parity also informs the exam, since a parous cervix and uterus feel different on bimanual exam. Ask specifically about ectopics, miscarriages, and deliveries, not just 'any pregnancies,' because patients often do not count early losses.

exam.maneuver: Vital signs: blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, respiratory rate
exam.meaning: Hypotension and tachycardia with pelvic pain and a positive pregnancy test mean hemorrhagic shock from ruptured ectopic — resuscitate and get OB/GYN to the bedside now. Fever points to PID or tubo-ovarian abscess. Stable vitals do not rule out torsion or early ectopic, but unstable vitals end the clinic visit and start the emergency pathway.

exam.maneuver: General appearance: note pallor, diaphoresis, distress level, and mental status
exam.meaning: A pale, diaphoretic, anxious patient with pelvic pain looks like blood loss even before the vitals declare it — trust the gestalt and move fast. A comfortable patient in no distress is reassuring but does not exclude torsion, which can present with intermittent pain between episodes. Document how she looks; it is part of the record that justifies your urgency or your reassurance.

exam.maneuver: Abdominal exam: inspect, then palpate all quadrants for tenderness, rebound, guarding, and masses
exam.meaning: Diffuse lower abdominal tenderness with rebound or guarding suggests peritonitis — from ruptured ectopic blood, ruptured tubo-ovarian abscess, or PID with peritonitis — and pushes toward emergent evaluation and imaging. Focal unilateral tenderness points to an ovarian source like torsion or a hemorrhagic cyst. A soft nontender abdomen makes a surgical emergency less likely and supports an outpatient workup.

exam.maneuver: Speculum exam: look for active bleeding and its source (cervical os vs vaginal walls), and for discharge
exam.meaning: Blood coming through the cervical os with a positive pregnancy test supports ectopic pregnancy or miscarriage and keeps you on the emergency pathway. Foul purulent discharge with fever supports PID and should prompt NAATs for chlamydia and gonorrhea. Identifying the bleeding source on speculum tells you whether the problem is uterine, cervical, or vaginal before you even do the bimanual exam.

exam.maneuver: Bimanual exam: move the cervix gently to assess for cervical motion tenderness
exam.meaning: Cervical motion tenderness is one of the clinical criteria for PID — with lower abdominal pain and discharge, it is enough to start empiric PID treatment with ceftriaxone plus doxycycline. Severe cervical motion tenderness with an adnexal mass and fever suggests tubo-ovarian abscess. Absent cervical motion tenderness does not rule out PID, but its presence commits you to treating.

exam.maneuver: Bimanual exam: assess uterine size, contour, mobility, and tenderness
exam.meaning: An enlarged, boggy, tender uterus suggests adenomyosis; a uniformly enlarged, irregular uterus suggests fibroids; a uterus larger than expected with a positive test raises multiple gestation or molar pregnancy. Uterine tenderness with fever supports endometritis or PID. Size and contour decide whether the ultrasound is for dating, fibroid mapping, or pregnancy evaluation.

exam.maneuver: Adnexal exam: palpate each adnexa for masses, noting size, tenderness, and mobility
exam.meaning: A tender adnexal mass with acute unilateral pain is ovarian torsion until proven otherwise — a surgical emergency where the ovary dies with time, so this finding triggers stat pelvic ultrasound with Doppler and a gynecology consult. A tender mass with fever suggests tubo-ovarian abscess; a tender adnexal fullness with a positive pregnancy test suggests ectopic. Document size, tenderness, and mobility; it determines whether she goes to ultrasound now or the OR.

exam.maneuver: Urine pregnancy test — obtain before any other testing or imaging decisions
exam.meaning: This is the first test in every pelvic pain workup in a person who could be pregnant — a positive test with pain and bleeding is ectopic until proven otherwise and changes the entire pathway to quantitative hCG and urgent ultrasound. A negative test lets you pursue the non-pregnant differential of torsion, PID, endometriosis, and fibroids without delay. Never skip it because the history sounds reassuring.

history.question: Do you want to become pregnant in the next year? What about longer term?
history.meaning: Whether she wants pregnancy in the next year, later, or never determines which methods fit — someone who wants pregnancy soon needs a short-acting or quickly reversible method, while someone done with childbearing can consider long-acting or permanent options. Ambivalence, the 'whatever happens' answer, argues for the most forgiving method since motivation to use it perfectly will be low. Document her timeline explicitly; it anchors the whole counseling visit.

history.question: Have you had unprotected sex in the last 5 days? When was your last period?
history.meaning: Unprotected sex in the last five days means emergency contraception is still on the table — the copper IUD is the most effective option, followed by ulipristal and then levonorgestrel — and the last menstrual period helps reasonably exclude pregnancy before a quick start. If pregnancy cannot be reasonably excluded, start the method anyway with backup contraception and a follow-up pregnancy test rather than making her wait weeks. This question prevents starting a routine method on top of an unrecognized pregnancy and captures the EC window before it closes.

history.question: What birth control have you used before, and why did you stop?
history.meaning: What she used before and why she stopped predicts what will work now — nausea on one pill may not recur on a different formulation or a non-systemic method, but a true contraindication like migraine with aura rules out all combined methods permanently. Prior method failures also reveal adherence patterns that argue for long-acting methods, which are the most effective precisely because they remove user error. Use her history to narrow the menu instead of starting from scratch.

history.question: Do you get migraines with aura — like visual changes, zigzags, or blind spots before a headache?
history.meaning: Migraine with aura is a contraindication to all combined estrogen-containing methods because of stroke risk — this is a hard stop under the US Medical Eligibility Criteria, not a preference. Progestin-only methods, hormonal IUDs, the copper IUD, and the implant remain safe options. Missing this question and prescribing a combined pill to someone with aura is a preventable serious error, so ask it explicitly every time.

history.question: Do you smoke cigarettes or vape? How old are you?
history.meaning: Smoking at age 35 or older is a contraindication to combined hormonal contraception because of cardiovascular and clot risk. Younger smokers can use combined methods but should be counseled to quit. If she is 35 or older and smokes, steer to progestin-only methods or IUDs and document the counseling — the age-plus-smoking combination is one of the most commonly missed contraindications.

history.question: Do you have high blood pressure, a history of blood clots, or a history of breast cancer?
listenFor: blood clot in my leg years ago
history.meaning: Hypertension, a history of venous thromboembolism, and current breast cancer are contraindications to estrogen-containing methods — these are the US Medical Eligibility Criteria red lines you must screen for. Progestin-only methods and IUDs are options when estrogen is off the table, with nuance around breast cancer history that deserves specialist input. Ask directly; patients often do not volunteer a clot from years ago unless prompted.

history.question: Are you breastfeeding, or did you recently give birth? When did you deliver?
history.meaning: Combined estrogen methods are avoided in the first 21 days postpartum because of clot risk, and breastfeeding preferences affect method choice since estrogen can reduce milk supply. Progestin-only methods and IUDs can be started much earlier, including immediately postpartum. Timing the method to her delivery date lets you offer a same-day start instead of a return visit that she may not make.

history.question: How important is it to have regular monthly periods — would you prefer lighter periods, or no periods at all?
history.meaning: Bleeding changes are the number one reason people stop contraception, so ask upfront: hormonal IUDs often lead to lighter periods or amenorrhea, the implant and depot shot commonly cause irregular spotting, and the copper IUD typically makes periods heavier and crampier. Matching the method to whether she wants monthly bleeding, no bleeding, or does not care prevents discontinuation. Set expectations before she starts, not after she bleeds and stops the method.

history.question: How long do you want this method to last? Is it important that it's reversible?
history.meaning: How long she wants coverage decides between methods lasting 3 to 10 years — IUDs and the implant, the long-acting reversible methods — versus daily, weekly, or monthly methods. Reassure her that IUDs and the implant are fully reversible with rapid return to fertility after removal, which is the commonest misconception blocking uptake. If she wants pregnancy within a year or two, the depot shot is a poor fit because return to fertility can be delayed for many months after the last injection.

history.question: Do you need protection against sexually transmitted infections?
history.meaning: No hormonal method or IUD protects against STIs, so anyone with STI risk still needs condoms — this counseling is non-negotiable, especially with new or multiple partners. Dual method use, an IUD or implant plus condoms, gives the best pregnancy and STI protection together. Document that you counseled on condoms so the visit record shows the STI conversation happened.

history.question: Are you on any prescription medications, especially seizure medications, rifampin, or St. John's wort? Any drug allergies?
history.meaning: Enzyme-inducing drugs — certain seizure medications, rifampin, and St. John's wort — reduce hormonal contraceptive effectiveness and may require an IUD instead, since IUDs work locally and are not affected. Latex allergy affects condom and diaphragm counseling. Ask about all prescription drugs, over-the-counter products, and supplements, since patients rarely connect their seizure medication to their birth control on their own.

history.question: How do you feel about remembering a daily pill — would you prefer something you don't have to think about?
history.meaning: A method she will actually use beats a theoretically better one she will forget — daily pills fail most often from missed doses, so a chaotic schedule argues for a weekly patch, monthly ring, or better yet a long-acting method. Long-acting reversible methods sit at the top of the efficacy tiers precisely because they eliminate daily action. Match the method to her life, not the other way around, and say the efficacy tiers out loud so she can weigh convenience against effectiveness.

exam.maneuver: Blood pressure measurement, seated, before prescribing
exam.meaning: Blood pressure is required before starting any combined estrogen-containing method — uncontrolled hypertension is a contraindication and you need a baseline to monitor on follow-up. If the blood pressure is elevated, do not start a combined method; choose a progestin-only method or an IUD and address the hypertension separately. Document the reading; it is the one exam finding that directly permits or blocks the prescription.

exam.maneuver: Weight and BMI
exam.meaning: Weight and BMI inform counseling: effectiveness of some methods, like emergency contraceptive pills and possibly the patch, decreases at higher weight, and weight is worth tracking since some methods are associated with weight change. BMI also matters for procedure planning for IUD or implant placement. Counsel on what the evidence supports without overstating it — frame weight as one factor in method selection, not a barrier to contraception.

exam.maneuver: Confirm and document that no pelvic exam is required before starting contraception
findings: pelvic exam not performed, not required
patient requests exam for other concerns
exam.meaning: A pelvic exam, Pap smear, or STI test is not required before starting contraception — requiring one is a barrier that delays care without improving safety. Same-day starts are standard: screen with history, check blood pressure, reasonably exclude pregnancy, and start. Document that you offered a same-day start and she was not required to undress for birth control.

exam.maneuver: Urine pregnancy test to reasonably exclude pregnancy before starting
exam.meaning: Reasonably excluding pregnancy before starting is the standard — a negative test with a consistent history lets you quick-start any method today, with backup contraception for the first week when backup is needed (for example, with combined methods started off-cycle). If the test is positive, stop and pivot to pregnancy options counseling. When pregnancy cannot be fully excluded but is unlikely, start the method with backup and a repeat test in two to four weeks rather than turning her away.

exam.maneuver: Appearance: grooming and hygiene; clothing (type, appropriateness); jewelry and makeup; scars, piercings, tattoos; dentition; assistive devices; other: diaphoresis, lacrimation, flushing.

phrases.Appropriate for weather and setting: Dressed appropriately for the weather and setting

phrases.None noted: No scars, piercings, or tattoos noted

exam.meaning: What you can see before the patient says a word: how they are groomed and dressed, and visible signs such as scars, tattoos, assistive devices, sweating, tearing, or flushing.

exam.maneuver: Behavior: posture; eye contact; gait; activity level: psychomotor slowing or agitation; abnormal movements, such as tremors, tics, or dystonias.
findings: Activity level: psychomotor slowing or agitation
Abnormal movements, such as tremors, tics, or dystonias
exam.meaning: How the patient carries and moves their body during the encounter: posture, eye contact, gait, overall activity level, and any abnormal movements.

exam.maneuver: Cooperation and attitude: how the patient relates to the examiner: cooperative, uncooperative, hostile, guarded, suspicious, or eager to please.
exam.meaning: How the patient relates to you as the examiner sets the frame for everything else in the interview, so name it plainly rather than leaving it implied.

exam.maneuver: Speech: rate: pressured, rapid, regular, slow; volume; articulation: dysarthria or stuttering; latency (pauses before speaking); quantity: mutism, paucity; prosody: intonation, rhythm.
findings: Rate: pressured, rapid, regular, or slow
exam.meaning: How the patient talks, separate from what they say: rate, volume, articulation, the pauses before they speak, how much they say, and the intonation and rhythm of their voice.

exam.maneuver: Mood and affect: mood is the patient's description of their feelings, in their own words; affect is the physical expression of the immediate feeling state.
findings: Mood, in the patient's own words
Affect, the observed physical expression of the immediate feeling state
exam.meaning: Mood is what the patient tells you they feel, in their own words. Affect is the feeling state you can see on them right now. Record both; they do not always match.

exam.maneuver: Qualities of affect: type: euthymic, elevated/euphoric, dysphoric, irritable, anxious, indifferent; range: intense/expansive > full > constricted > blunted > flat; lability: rapidity of affect change; appropriateness to content.
findings: Type: euthymic, elevated/euphoric, dysphoric, irritable, anxious, indifferent
Range: intense/expansive > full > constricted > blunted > flat
exam.meaning: Describe affect on four points: its type, its range from intense or expansive down to flat, how rapidly it changes, and whether it fits what the patient is talking about.

exam.maneuver: Thought process: spectrum: goal-directed → circumstantial → tangential → loosening of associations → flight of ideas; thought blocking: abrupt cessation of one's train of thought.
findings: Thought blocking: abrupt cessation of one's train of thought
exam.meaning: How the patient's thoughts connect as they speak, placed on the spectrum from goal-directed to flight of ideas. Note thought blocking when the train of thought stops abruptly.

exam.maneuver: Thought content: suicidal or self-harm ideation; homicidal or violent ideation; delusions: fixed, false beliefs that are outside of cultural or societal norms; obsessions.
findings: Delusions: fixed, false beliefs that are outside of cultural or societal norms

fields.label: Suicidal or self-harm ideation
fields.detailHint: Passive or active; plan, intent, means

exam.meaning: What the patient is thinking about, asked about directly: thoughts of harming themselves or others, delusions, and obsessions. These do not surface on their own; you have to ask.

exam.maneuver: Perception: illusions: misinterpretation of sensory stimulus; hallucinations: visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, gustatory; dissociative symptoms: depersonalization (feeling detached from one's own body) or derealization (feeling detached from one's surroundings).
findings: Hallucinations: visual, auditory, tactile, olfactory, gustatory
Depersonalization (feeling detached from one's own body)
exam.meaning: Whether the patient misreads a real stimulus (an illusion), perceives something that is not there (a hallucination, in any sense), or feels detached from their own body or from their surroundings.

exam.maneuver: Cognition: general consciousness; orientation; attention (serial 7s, days of week or months of year forwards and backwards); memory; visuospatial ability: clock drawing, transparent cube; abstraction: similarity between objects, proverb understanding.
findings: Attention (serial 7s, days of week or months of year forwards and backwards)
Visuospatial ability: clock drawing, transparent cube
Abstraction: similarity between objects, proverb understanding

fields.label: Attention
fields.detailHint: Serial 7s result; days or months forwards and backwards

exam.how: Can use standardized tools like the MMSE or MoCA.
exam.meaning: The thinking domains to test one by one: consciousness, orientation, attention, memory, visuospatial ability, and abstraction.

exam.maneuver: Insight and judgment: insight is the patient's understanding of illness, treatment, or behavior; judgment is the patient's decision-making ability, the actions the individual will take based on insight.
findings: Insight: understanding of illness, treatment, or behavior
Judgment: decision-making ability, and the actions taken based on insight
exam.meaning: Insight is whether the patient understands their illness, treatment, or behavior. Judgment is what they will do with that understanding: their decision-making ability in action.

sheets.title: Decision-Making Capacity and Informed Consent (Sliding Scale)

history.question: Now that we have talked through the options, which treatment have you decided on?
listenFor: States one clear choice and stays with it
States a choice but changes it when the question is repeated
Gives different choices to different people
history.meaning: Expressing a choice is the floor of the four abilities, and it is the only ability a tier 1 (awareness and assent) decision requires beyond simple awareness. A choice that flips between tellings is not yet a decision anyone can act on, and a patient who cannot state a choice at all needs a surrogate for that decision no matter how well they chat. Ask it plainly and write down the answer in the patient's words.

history.question: Is this your own decision, or is someone else making it for you?
listenFor: Own decision, but clearly influenced by family or staff pressure
Going along only out of fear of displeasing the team
history.meaning: A capable patient's choice still fails as consent if it is not voluntary. Pressure usually comes from family, not staff, and the fix is often a private conversation rather than a capacity fight. If the words are the patient's but the will is someone else's, the consent is not valid even when every other ability is intact.

history.question: Can you tell me in your own words what your medical problem is, and what this treatment is meant to do?
listenFor: Accurately restates the diagnosis and the purpose of the treatment
Restates the basics with minor gaps
Cannot restate the diagnosis or what the treatment does
history.meaning: Understanding is teach-back, not nodding. Patients who cannot repeat the facts back were usually never taught them in usable form, so re-teach in plain language, with an interpreter if needed, and test again before scoring this as a failure. This is the ability that mild cognitive impairment erodes first, and it is the core of Drane's tier 2 and of Appelbaum's framework.

history.question: What are the main risks and benefits of this treatment? What other choices do you have, including not having the treatment at all?
listenFor: Names the major risks, benefits, and alternatives, including no treatment
Names benefits but few risks or alternatives
Names a risk or benefit only after prompting
Cannot name any risk, benefit, or alternative
history.meaning: A patient who can describe the treatment but not its alternatives has not been given a decision yet. The no-treatment option is the one most often skipped in disclosure and the one refusals turn on, because refusing means choosing it. If the patient cannot name it, the disclosure was incomplete and the assessment is not fair until it is repeated.

history.question: Do you believe you actually have this condition, and that treatment could help you?
listenFor: Acknowledges the condition and that treatment could help
Acknowledges the condition but doubts treatment will help
Acknowledges symptoms but blames an unrelated cause
Denies being ill at all despite the evidence
history.meaning: Appreciation is where understanding stops being a quiz about facts and becomes about this patient's own life. A patient can recite a diagnosis perfectly and still fail here, because the facts never land as true for them; this is the classic failure in psychosis and in anosognosia after brain injury. Doubting that a treatment will work is not by itself a failure; denying the condition exists, on the basis of a fixed false belief, is.

history.question: What do you think will happen to you if you have this treatment, and what will happen if you do not?
listenFor: Realistically applies both outcomes to himself or herself
Accepts the outcomes in general but doubts they apply to him or her
Acknowledges the outcome of treatment but not of refusing it
Believes nothing bad can happen whatever is decided
history.meaning: This is the question that separates a risky preference from an incapacity. A patient who says the untreated outcome is death, believes it, and chooses it anyway for reasons of their own is exercising capacity at the highest tier. A patient who agrees the risk is real for other people but impossible for them has not appreciated the decision, and that gap is what tier 3 exists to catch.

history.question: Why did you pick this option over the others?
listenFor: Compares the options and gives reasons tied to the facts discussed
Gives a reason, but it rests on a factual misunderstanding
Reasons jump between unrelated ideas and the conclusion does not follow
Choice follows directly from a fixed false belief rather than the facts
history.meaning: Reasoning is judged on the process, never on whether the conclusion matches the team's recommendation. A conclusion the team hates, reached by weighing real facts against the patient's own values, passes. A conclusion the team loves, reached by echoing the last person who spoke, does not. A factual misunderstanding is fixable by teaching; reasoning that runs on a delusion is not.

history.question: Walk me through how you got from what we discussed to this decision.
listenFor: Logical sequence from the facts to the conclusion
Illogical leaps; the conclusion does not follow from the facts given
No process to describe; the decision is impulsive or copies the last suggestion
history.meaning: Asking for the path, not just the reason, exposes failures the first reasoning question can miss: thought disorder, severe concrete thinking, and decisions made by suggestion in patients eager to please. Minor gaps are normal in frightened, sick people and do not fail anyone. What fails a patient at a high tier is a path that does not connect the facts to the choice at all.

exam.maneuver: Name the one specific decision being assessed, in a single sentence, before asking anything else.
findings: One specific decision identified, for this treatment at this time
Several decisions bundled together; they need separate assessments
Decision never pinned down; the assessment drifted into a global judgment of the patient
exam.meaning: Capacity attaches to a decision, not to a person. A global verdict (this patient has no capacity) is almost always wrong, because the same patient may decide simple things well and complex ones badly. Every later step, the disclosure, the four abilities, the threshold, only makes sense against one named decision.

exam.maneuver: Rate what is at stake: how likely and how bad is the harm if this choice goes wrong, weighed against the benefit the choice could bring.
findings: Low stakes: the outcome is similar whichever way the patient chooses
Moderate stakes: real harm is possible but unlikely, or likely but limited
High stakes: death or serious, lasting harm is likely if the choice goes wrong
exam.meaning: This rating is the input to the sliding scale, and Buchanan and Brock are explicit that it is the expected harm of acting on the patient's choice that moves the standard. Rate the decision in front of you, not the disease in general: the same operation is low stakes for a patient with good alternatives and high stakes for one with none.

exam.maneuver: Note whether the patient is accepting or refusing the recommended course, and let that set which end of the scale you are on.
findings: Accepting a recommended treatment with a favorable balance: lowest showing required
Choosing between options of similar balance, or the balance is genuinely uncertain: middle showing
Refusing a recommended treatment with a favorable balance, or accepting a dangerous one: highest showing required
exam.meaning: This is the asymmetry Buchanan and Brock draw out of the risk-related standard: consenting and refusing the same treatment are different decisions with different stakes, so they carry different bars.
