It is also the step that protects against the commonest error, probing capacity only when the patient disagrees. A patient who cheerfully accepts a dangerous, futile procedure deserves the same scrutiny as one who refuses a safe one.

exam.maneuver: State the tier out loud, and in the note, before judging the four abilities.
findings: Tier 1 applies: awareness and assent (Drane standard 1)
Tier 2 applies: understanding, with a choice based on weighing risks and benefits (Drane standard 2)
Tier 3 applies: appreciation and rational reasoning about the consequences for the patient's own life (Drane standard 3)
exam.meaning: Fixing the bar before the test is what keeps the sliding scale honest. If the threshold is chosen after hearing the answers, it silently becomes an outcome test: high when the patient refuses, low when the patient agrees. Writing the tier down first also tells the next clinician exactly what showing was required, which is what a reviewing court or consultant will look for.

exam.maneuver: Disclose before you judge: the diagnosis, what the treatment is and what it is for, its material risks and benefits, the reasonable alternatives, and the option of no treatment.
findings: All elements disclosed in plain language, with teach-back
Disclosed, but in jargon, too fast, or without an interpreter the patient needed
Risks or alternatives not yet disclosed; the patient cannot fairly be assessed yet
exam.how: Cover all five elements, then ask the patient to teach them back. Disclosure is an element of valid consent in its own right (StatPearls lists disclosure, capacity, and voluntariness as the three elements), and a failed teach-back after good disclosure means something different from a failed teach-back after a rushed one.
exam.meaning: Capacity testing on undisclosed information measures the disclosure, not the patient. Most apparent understanding failures in hospital practice are teaching failures: wrong language, wrong hour, wrong person in the room. Redo the disclosure properly before concluding anything, and document that you did.

exam.maneuver: Check whether a recognized exception applies before skipping or overriding consent: true emergency, the patient's own waiver, or therapeutic privilege.
findings: No exception applies: the decision of a patient with capacity governs
True emergency: treatment needed now to prevent death or serious harm, patient cannot consent, no surrogate reachable
Waiver: the patient has chosen not to be informed and has delegated the decision
Therapeutic privilege claimed: disclosure itself would cause this patient serious harm
exam.meaning: Each exception is narrower than its reputation. The emergency exception covers the emergency only. A waiver must be the patient's own voluntary act. Therapeutic privilege is about harm from the information itself, never about the fear that an informed patient will refuse; modern sources treat it as rare, and invoking it without documenting the specific expected harm is indefensible. Lack of capacity is not on this list on purpose: it routes the decision to a surrogate, it does not erase consent.

exam.maneuver: Optimize before concluding: treat pain, hypoxia, infection, and delirium; review sedating medications; pick the patient's best time of day; provide glasses, hearing aids, and an interpreter; offer a trusted person's presence.
findings: Reversible barriers treated or excluded; assessment done at the patient's best
Barriers partly addressed; the showing may improve, so reassess before a final conclusion
Assessment done while a reversible barrier was active; the conclusion is not yet reliable
exam.meaning: A capacity verdict reached on a delirious, sedated, or pain-wracked patient at 3 a.m. is a verdict about the barrier, not the patient. Because capacity fluctuates, the ethical move is to remove what can be removed and test again. Documenting the barriers you addressed is also what separates a defensible assessment from a one-line opinion.

exam.maneuver: Plan the reassessment: capacity is decision-specific and can change, so state when and why this conclusion should be revisited.
findings: Showing stable across repeat checks; no early reassessment needed
Showing fluctuates with symptoms, time of day, or treatment; reassess at the time of the decision
Showing improved after the underlying cause was treated; the earlier conclusion is superseded
exam.meaning: Yesterday's incapacity is not today's. A patient who lacked capacity during delirium may regain it as the infection clears, and their own decisions then govern again, including decisions that undo what a surrogate chose. Building the reassessment trigger into the note (if the fever resolves, if the morning dose wears off) keeps the team from treating a temporary state as a permanent label.

exam.maneuver: Conclude against the preset tier and write the note: the decision, the disclosure given, the patient's performance on each of the four abilities in the patient's own words, the tier applied, and the conclusion.
findings: Meets the required showing: the patient has capacity for this decision and the choice governs
Borderline: abilities are partial; add support, involve psychiatry or ethics, and reassess rather than forcing a binary call now
Does not meet the required showing for this decision: the patient lacks capacity for this decision; move to the surrogate process
exam.how: Quote the patient verbatim at least once per ability that decided the outcome. Appelbaum's documentation standard is a description of the disclosure, the consequences of the choice, the patient's mental status, performance on the four abilities, and the conclusion; a conclusion with no quoted words cannot be checked by anyone who reads it later.
exam.meaning: The conclusion must name the decision (capacity for this decision), never the person. A borderline result is a real result: at a low tier, partial abilities may still clear the bar; at tier 3 they do not, and the honest chart entry is what was shown, what tier was required, and what happens next. Forcing a binary call on a borderline showing, in either direction, is how both autonomy violations and preventable harms happen.

exam.maneuver: If the patient lacks capacity for this decision, identify who decides and by what standard.
findings: An advance directive or appointed agent names the decision-maker
No agent: use the applicable surrogate process, asking first what the patient would have wanted (substituted judgment), then best interests
No surrogate available and the decision cannot wait: emergency treatment only, while guardianship or court routes are started for anything beyond it
exam.meaning: The surrogate's first job is to speak in the patient's voice, using the patient's known wishes and values; best interests is the fallback when those are unknown, not the default. Who counts as a surrogate, and in what order, is set by law and institutional policy and varies by jurisdiction, so this sheet deliberately names no state's list; check the local rule before relying on a family member's say-so for a major decision.

history.question: When did you have your first drink, and how has your drinking changed since then?
listenFor: First drink in late adolescence or adulthood, use never escalated
First drink in early adolescence, gradual escalation over years
Rapid escalation to heavy use within the first year of drinking
history.meaning: Age of first use and the speed of escalation are prognostic. Drinking that starts before the mid-teens and escalates fast is associated with a more severe, more relapsing course, and it changes how hard you push for structured treatment rather than brief advice. Record the actual age of first use in the detail field.

history.question: In the past three months, how much and how often have you been drinking? Walk me through a typical day.
listenFor: No drinking in the past three months
Drinks less than weekly, within low-risk limits
Weekly heavy drinking days (binge pattern, sober days between)
Daily heavy drinking, including morning drinking
history.meaning: Pattern matters as much as volume. Daily drinking with morning relief drinking signals physical dependence and withdrawal risk; a binge pattern with sober days carries different risks (injury, arrhythmia, pancreatitis) and a lower immediate withdrawal risk. Put the actual amount in the detail field in standard drinks per day, and note the largest amount in a single day.

history.question: How do you take alcohol in (beer, wine, spirits), and have you ever drunk non-beverage alcohol such as mouthwash or hand sanitizer?
listenFor: Has drunk non-beverage alcohol (mouthwash, sanitizer, rubbing alcohol) when drinks were unavailable
history.meaning: Route for alcohol is beverage type plus this one escalation question. Drinking non-beverage alcohol is a severity marker: it means withdrawal avoidance outweighed taste, cost, and safety, and it adds methanol and isopropanol exposure to the medical picture. Ask it without surprise or judgment in your voice, or it will not be answered honestly.

history.question: When was your last drink, and what is the longest you have gone without drinking since your use became heavy?
listenFor: Last drink more than a year ago
Last drink weeks to months ago
Last drink within the past week
Drank today or yesterday, no sustained period without drinking since use became heavy
history.meaning: Last drink sets the withdrawal clock: symptoms start 6 to 12 hours after the last drink or a sharp reduction, seizures cluster at 24 to 48 hours, and delirium tremens at 48 to 96 hours. Longest abstinence is the optimistic counterpart, proof the patient has done it before, and the circumstances of that period (treatment, incarceration, pregnancy, willpower) tell you what to rebuild.

history.question: What happens when you stop or cut down? Have you ever had shakes, seizures, hallucinations, or delirium tremens (the DTs)?
listenFor: Mild withdrawal: shakes, sweating, anxiety, nausea, insomnia
Moderate withdrawal: vomiting, racing heart, hallucinations while still oriented
Severe withdrawal history: withdrawal seizure, delirium tremens, or ICU care for withdrawal
history.meaning: Past withdrawal severity is the best predictor of this episode's withdrawal severity, and it drives the level-of-care decision more than today's CIWA-Ar score does. A prior withdrawal seizure or DTs moves the patient toward medically managed inpatient withdrawal management even if they currently look comfortable. Each episode of untreated withdrawal also makes the next one worse (kindling), which is a concrete reason to treat this episode fully.

history.question: When did you first use opioids, and how did you get from that first use to what you are using now?
listenFor: Started with prescribed pain medication, dose escalated over time
Started with heroin or illicit fentanyl
Started with pills obtained from friends, family, or dealers, later switched to heroin or fentanyl for cost
history.meaning: The pathway matters for trust and for treatment. A patient whose use began with a legitimate prescription often carries shame and a pain problem that still needs a plan; a patient who switched from pills to fentanyl for cost has usually crossed into higher overdose risk. Record the current drug by name in the detail field, and assume street opioids contain fentanyl unless the patient has evidence otherwise.

history.question: In the past three months, how much and how often have you used? What does a day look like?
listenFor: No opioid use in the past three months
Daily use, escalating amount, using mainly to avoid feeling sick
history.meaning: Using to avoid withdrawal rather than to get high marks the shift from impulsive to compulsive use and usually means opioid use disorder is at least moderate. Put the amount in the detail field in the units the patient uses (bags, pills, dollars per day) and convert cautiously; street fentanyl potency varies so widely that dose comparisons are rough. Frequency also sets expectations for how fast withdrawal will start.

history.question: How do you use (swallow, snort, smoke, inject)? If you inject, do you share or reuse equipment?
listenFor: Injects, uses own sterile equipment, does not share
Injects with reused or shared equipment
history.meaning: Route changes the medical workup. Injection use, especially with sharing, mandates screening for HIV, hepatitis C, endocarditis, and skin and soft-tissue infection, and a look at the injection sites during the exam. A move from snorting to injecting is an escalation point worth naming in the assessment, and every injecting patient should leave with naloxone and a fentanyl test strip conversation.

history.question: When did you last use, and what is the longest you have gone without opioids?
listenFor: Last use more than a year ago
Last use weeks to months ago
Last use within the past 24 hours
Used today; no sustained abstinence since use became daily
history.meaning: Last use, plus which opioid, sets the withdrawal timeline: heroin and short-acting pills declare themselves within 8 to 12 hours, methadone may take 36 hours or more, and fentanyl is erratic because it stores in fat and leaches back out. It also sets buprenorphine timing, which is scored with the COWS worksheet. Longest abstinence and what supported it belong in the treatment plan.

history.question: What does opioid withdrawal feel like for you, and have you ever overdosed or needed naloxone (Narcan)?
listenFor: Withdrawal: aches, sweating, GI upset, insomnia, craving, never overdosed
Withdrawal plus one prior overdose reversed with naloxone or by bystanders
Multiple prior overdoses, or an overdose requiring intubation or ICU care
history.meaning: Overdose history is the strongest single predictor of a future fatal overdose, and a prior reversal is an opening to prescribe naloxone and teach whoever the patient uses with. Ask who gave the naloxone and whether the patient now carries it. Note also that tolerance drops fast during abstinence, so the weeks after detox, incarceration, or this admission are the highest-risk window.

history.question: When did you first use stimulants (cocaine, methamphetamine, or prescription stimulants not as prescribed), and which ones?
listenFor: Prescription stimulants used non-medically, or several stimulant types
history.meaning: Name the actual drug in the detail field; cocaine, methamphetamine, and diverted prescription stimulants share a syndrome but differ in duration, and methamphetamine's long half-life drives the prolonged agitation and psychosis seen on this service. Record when use started and whether stimulant use is tied to staying awake for work or to sex, both of which shape the plan.

history.question: In the past three months, how often have you used, and do you use in runs or binges?
listenFor: No stimulant use in the past three months
Binge runs lasting days with little or no sleep
history.meaning: The binge pattern is the stimulant signature: redosing for one to three days, then crashing. Days awake is a number worth recording in the detail field, because sleep deprivation alone produces paranoia and hallucinations that usually clear with sleep, which separates them from a primary psychotic disorder in the differential.

history.question: How do you use (snort, smoke, inject, swallow)?
history.meaning: Smoked and injected stimulants reach the brain in seconds and carry the highest addiction liability and the same bloodborne infection risks as opioid injection. Ask injecting patients the equipment-sharing questions from the opioid battery rather than assuming the answers carry over.

history.question: When did you last use, and what is the longest you have gone without?
listenFor: Last use more than a year ago
Last use weeks to months ago
Last use within the past few days
Used today or yesterday, still coming down
history.meaning: Last use tells you whether today's agitation or paranoia is intoxication, the crash, or something else. A patient still coming down mainly needs sleep, food, and a quiet room; documenting the timeline prevents that presentation from being misread as new mania or schizophrenia.

history.question: What happens when you come down or stop? Have you ever become paranoid, heard or seen things, had chest pain, or had a seizure while using or coming down?
listenFor: Crash: prolonged sleep, low mood, increased appetite, strong craving
Paranoia or hallucinations during use or the crash, cleared with sleep
Severe complications: chest pain or MI, seizure, or psychosis that persisted after sleep
history.meaning: There is no dangerous autonomic withdrawal from stimulants; the crash is hypersomnia, dysphoria, and craving, and suicide risk rises in it, so ask about mood directly. Psychosis that persists well beyond sleep and last use changes the diagnosis conversation. Chest pain on stimulants is an MI workup, not a withdrawal symptom.

history.question: When did you start using cannabis, and what form do you use (flower, edibles, vapes or concentrates, synthetic products such as K2 or Spice)?
listenFor: Flower only, started in adolescence or later
High-potency products (vaped concentrates, dabs, edibles) as the main form
history.meaning: Form is the clinically important detail now. High-potency concentrates and daily use are the patterns linked to psychosis risk and to cannabinoid hyperemesis, and synthetic cannabinoids are a different drug class in effect, with agitation, psychosis, and kidney injury that flower does not cause. Record the form and potency in the detail field.

history.question: In the past three months, how often have you used, and how much in a typical day?
listenFor: No cannabis use in the past three months
Weekly to several times a week
Daily or near-daily use, including use to sleep or to get through the day
history.meaning: Daily use, morning use, and use to sleep or eat are the markers of cannabis use disorder rather than recreational use. Amount is hard to compare across products, so record the patient's own units (joints, grams, carts per week) in the detail field and track change in those units.

history.question: How do you use (smoke, vape, edibles)?
history.meaning: Route sets onset and duration, which matters when a patient's presentation includes panic or prolonged intoxication after edibles, whose effects arrive late and last far longer than smoked cannabis. Vaped concentrates deliver the highest doses and are the route most associated with heavy daily use.

history.question: When did you last use, and what is the longest you have gone without?
listenFor: Last use more than a year ago
Last use weeks to months ago
Last use within the past week
Used today; daily use with no sustained break
history.meaning: Last use also explains the drug screen: THC from daily use stays positive for weeks, so a positive result does not date the use. Longest abstinence and what interrupted it (a job drug test, pregnancy, a psychotic episode) are useful levers for the treatment conversation.

history.question: What happens when you stop? Have you had repeated vomiting episodes that hot showers relieve?
listenFor: Withdrawal: irritability, anger, poor sleep and vivid dreams, decreased appetite, restlessness
Cannabinoid hyperemesis pattern: cyclic vomiting relieved by hot bathing
history.meaning: Cannabis withdrawal is real, peaks at two to six days, and is a common unrecognized reason daily users resume. The hyperemesis pattern is asked about explicitly because patients rarely connect vomiting to cannabis, and the hot-shower detail is close to diagnostic; the only effective treatment is stopping, which the patient needs to hear plainly.

history.question: Do you smoke cigarettes or use other tobacco or nicotine (vape, smokeless)? When did you start?
listenFor: Denies any tobacco or nicotine use
Former smoker, quit more than a year ago
Current use of vaping products or smokeless tobacco only
history.meaning: Tobacco is easy to skip on an addiction service and expensive to skip: nicotine withdrawal on a locked unit without replacement makes patients irritable and gets charted as agitation. Record the product and start age in the detail field, and note that people with substance use disorders die more often from tobacco than from their presenting drug.

history.question: How much do you smoke in a day, and how soon after waking is your first cigarette?
listenFor: Less than half a pack a day, first cigarette more than an hour after waking
About a pack a day, first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking
More than a pack a day, first cigarette within 5 minutes of waking, wakes at night to smoke
history.meaning: Time to the first cigarette is the single best bedside gauge of nicotine dependence and is one of the two Heaviness of Smoking Index items. Within five minutes means heavy dependence: start adequate nicotine replacement on admission rather than waiting for the patient to ask, and expect withdrawal to color every other interview that day.

history.question: How do you use tobacco or nicotine (cigarettes, cigars, vape, smokeless, pouches)?
history.meaning: Route determines replacement: patches replace a steady nicotine level, gum or lozenges cover breakthrough craving, and a patient whose main use is vaping may need both. Smokeless use also means checking the mouth during the exam.

history.question: When did you last smoke or use nicotine, and what is the longest quit you have had?
listenFor: Last use more than a year ago
Last use weeks to months ago
Smoked today, within the past few hours
Smoked within the last hour; no quit longer than a few days
history.meaning: Nicotine withdrawal starts within hours, so 'smoked within the last hour' versus 'smoked this morning' changes how much of today's irritability and poor concentration is withdrawal. Prior quits, especially ones supported by medication, predict what will work this time and are worth recording with what ended them.

history.question: What happens when you cannot smoke? Have you ever quit with medication or counseling, and what happened?
listenFor: Irritability, anxiety, restlessness, poor concentration, increased appetite
Prior quit attempts ended by withdrawal symptoms or cravings within days
history.meaning: Most quit attempts fail on withdrawal and craving in the first week, which is treatable. A history of quitting attempts that collapsed in days is an argument for combination nicotine replacement or varenicline this admission, not for more willpower.

history.question: Do you take sedatives such as benzodiazepines (Xanax, Klonopin, Valium, Ativan) or sleep medicines beyond how they were prescribed, or get them from another source? When did that start?
listenFor: Denies any sedative misuse; takes prescribed sedatives exactly as directed
Takes a prescribed benzodiazepine in larger amounts or more often than prescribed
Buys benzodiazepines or other sedatives illicitly
Uses sedatives specifically to come down from stimulants or to manage alcohol or opioid withdrawal
history.meaning: Ask about prescribed and illicit use in one breath, because patients do not count dose escalation of their own prescription as misuse. The reason for use sorts the problem: sedatives used to self-manage alcohol withdrawal or stimulant crashes mean the sedative problem will outlast detox unless the underlying cycle is treated.

history.question: In the past three months, how much and how often have you taken? What is the most you have taken in a day?
listenFor: No sedative misuse in the past three months
Daily use at or near prescribed-equivalent doses
Daily high-dose use, escalating, with periods of amnesia or blackouts
history.meaning: Record the drug and daily amount in the detail field, converting to a rough diazepam equivalent if you can, because benzodiazepine withdrawal planning is dose-based. Blackouts and amnesia signal high doses and are also when injuries and unwanted sexual exposure happen, which the patient may need help disclosing.

history.question: How do you take them (by mouth, snorted, injected)?
listenFor: Injects, or combines with opioids or alcohol to boost effect
history.meaning: Non-oral routes and deliberate co-use with opioids or alcohol are severity and overdose markers: benzodiazepines plus opioids is one of the most common combinations in fatal overdose, because each removes the other's safety margin. A patient in this group needs naloxone and explicit counseling even if opioids are not their primary drug.

history.question: When did you last take a sedative, and what is the longest you have gone without?
listenFor: Last misuse more than a year ago
Last use weeks to months ago
Last use within the past 24 hours
Used today; cannot recall a sustained period without
history.meaning: Timing depends on the agent: withdrawal from short-acting agents such as alprazolam can start within a day, while clonazepam and diazepam withdrawal may not declare itself for several days, so a comfortable day one does not clear the patient. Last use plus agent plus dose is the minimum needed to plan a taper versus inpatient management.

history.question: What happens when you stop suddenly? Have you ever had a seizure, severe anxiety and tremor, hallucinations, or needed hospital care when you ran out?
listenFor: Rebound anxiety and insomnia worse than baseline
Withdrawal: tremor, sweating, racing heart, perceptual symptoms
Severe withdrawal history: seizure, delirium, or hospital or ICU care for sedative withdrawal
history.meaning: Benzodiazepine withdrawal, like alcohol withdrawal, can kill, and abrupt cessation after long high-dose use is the setup for seizures. A prior withdrawal seizure means this patient gets a planned taper or substitution protocol, never an abrupt stop, including during this admission for an unrelated problem. Rebound anxiety in the first days should not be mistaken for the underlying anxiety disorder returning.

history.question: Has your use caused health problems (overdoses, infections, liver or heart problems, blackouts, injuries, hospital visits)?
listenFor: No medical consequences the patient is aware of
Minor consequences: blackouts, falls, missed doses of other medicines
Serious consequences: overdose, endocarditis, hepatitis C or HIV, liver disease, withdrawal complications
Life-threatening or disabling consequences, or currently in hospital because of use
history.meaning: This is ASAM dimension 2 territory: the biomedical list decides today's workup and how much medical risk the withdrawal plan carries. Patients under-report, so ask about specific events (falls, infections, hospital visits) rather than 'health problems' in the abstract, and reconcile with the chart afterward.

history.question: Has your use interfered with work, school, family roles, or responsibilities at home?
listenFor: Occasional missed obligations or impaired performance
Lost a job, failed classes, or lost housing or custody because of use
Currently unable to work or care for dependents because of use
history.meaning: Failed role obligations are a DSM-5 criterion and one of the NIDA-Modified ASSIST harm questions, and they are often the consequence the patient cares most about, which makes them the natural starting point for the readiness conversation. Concrete losses (a job, custody, housing) also define what recovery needs to protect first.

history.question: Has your use caused legal or money problems (arrests, DUI, probation, debt, spending money meant for other things)?
listenFor: Financial strain or debt from use
Legal consequences: DUI, possession charges, probation or parole
Current court mandate, pending charges, or use threatening parole or custody status
history.meaning: Legal status changes the frame of treatment: a court-mandated patient may engage for external reasons that still predict retention, and parole or custody deadlines can set the treatment timeline. Ask matter-of-factly; patients expect the question on an addiction service and read evasion as either naivety or judgment.

history.question: Has anyone close to you (family, friends, a doctor) expressed concern about your use or asked you to cut down?
listenFor: Family or friends have expressed concern
A clinician has advised cutting down or quitting
Concern from others is a major source of conflict, or the patient disputes that any problem exists
history.meaning: This is one of the ASSIST harm questions, and the gap between others' concern and the patient's own view is a working measure of where the patient is in recognizing the problem. It also identifies the people in the recovery environment (ASAM dimension 6): the concerned spouse is both a historian and a potential ally in the plan.

history.question: Where do you live and who do you live with? Do the people around you use, and is your housing stable?
listenFor: Stable housing, household members do not use
Stable housing, but household members or close contacts use
Unstable housing (couch surfing, shelter, transitional housing)
Homeless, or living environment centers on active use
history.meaning: Recovery environment is ASAM dimension 6 and it predicts relapse as strongly as the drug history does. The best detox fails if the patient returns to a house where everyone uses and there is nowhere else to sleep. This answer often decides between outpatient follow-up and a residential referral more than any other single item.

history.question: What treatment have you had before (detox, residential, intensive outpatient, counseling, mutual-help groups such as AA or NA)? What helped and what did not?
listenFor: Detox only, no continuing treatment afterward
One or more episodes of structured treatment (residential, IOP, outpatient)
Multiple treatment episodes including long-term recovery periods
history.meaning: Detox without continuing care is the most common failed pattern in this history, and naming it sets up the plan for this admission: the withdrawal management is the beginning, not the treatment. Ask what specifically helped, because patients return to what worked, and a prior two-year recovery is the strongest evidence about what to rebuild.

history.question: Have you ever taken medication for addiction (naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram, buprenorphine, methadone, nicotine replacement, varenicline)? What happened on it?
listenFor: Never offered or never tried medication treatment
Tried medication, stopped early because of side effects, access, or cost
Tried medication with a good response, later stopped and relapsed
Currently on medication treatment, or previously maintained long-term on it
history.meaning: A good prior response is the best guide to this admission's pharmacotherapy, and a stop for access or cost reasons is a systems problem the team can actually fix. Patients who 'failed' buprenorphine often mean the dose was too low or induction was precipitated and miserable; the detail of what happened matters more than the label.

history.question: Have you tried to cut down or stop on your own? What happened, and what was going on when you used again?
listenFor: Tried, relapsed quickly because of withdrawal symptoms or craving
Tried, sustained a period of abstinence, relapsed around a specific trigger
Multiple attempts; can name a consistent relapse pattern
history.meaning: Failed cut-down attempts are an ASSIST harm question and an ASAM dimension 5 (relapse potential) probe at the same time. The trigger the patient names (pain, insomnia, a place, a person, payday) is the relapse-prevention agenda. Relapse after withdrawal-driven failure argues for medication; relapse after a trigger argues for skills and environment change; most patients need both.

history.question: Where are you with your use right now: not thinking about changing, thinking about it, preparing, or already changing?
listenFor: Preparing to change, has a plan or a date (preparation)
Actively changing or maintaining a change already made (action or maintenance)
history.meaning: Readiness is ASAM dimension 4 and it sets the interview's job. A precontemplative patient needs information, a relationship, and an open door, not a discharge plan they will not follow; arguing at this stage mainly documents your frustration. Record the stage per substance if it differs, because patients are often ready to stop one drug and not another.

history.question: On a scale of 0 to 10, how important is it to you to change, and how confident are you that you could?
listenFor: Importance and confidence both low (0 to 3)
Importance and confidence both high (7 to 10)
history.meaning: The two rulers separate motivation from self-efficacy, and the treatment differs: high importance with low confidence needs past successes, small steps, and medication support, while low importance needs exploration of what the patient does want. Follow up with 'why that number and not a lower one' to importance, and 'what would move confidence up one point' to confidence, and put the actual numbers in the detail field.

history.question: What is your goal: complete abstinence, cutting down, using more safely, or are you not sure?
listenFor: Goal is complete abstinence from all substances
Goal is abstinence from the primary substance only
Goal is reduction or safer use, not abstinence
Undecided, or goal is set by someone else (court, family, employer)
history.meaning: Document the patient's goal in the patient's terms, even when it is not the goal you would choose. A reduction goal stated honestly is more workable than an abstinence goal stated to end the interview, and a mismatch between the patient's goal and the program's requirements should surface now rather than at discharge. Revisit the goal after withdrawal is treated, because goals stated while withdrawing are often narrower than goals stated comfortable.

exam.maneuver: Score nausea and vomiting.
findings: 7 - Constant nausea, frequent dry heaves, and vomiting
exam.how: Ask: "Do you feel sick to your stomach? Have you vomited?" Observation.
exam.meaning: Nausea and vomiting are usually the first symptoms to appear as alcohol levels fall, starting 6 to 12 hours after the last drink. The original scale anchors this item only at 0, 1, 4, and 7; scores of 2, 3, 5, and 6 are assigned by judging severity between anchors. Vomiting also blocks the oral route for benzodiazepines, so a high score here is one reason protocols switch to IV dosing.

exam.maneuver: Score tremor.
findings: 1 - Not visible, but can be felt at fingertips
7 - Severe, even with arms not extended
exam.how: Arms extended and fingers spread apart. Observation.
exam.meaning: Tremor is the most visible early sign of withdrawal and tracks autonomic overdrive as GABA inhibition falls away and glutamate rebounds. A tremor that is present at rest, without the arms extended, marks severe withdrawal. Score what you see at the moment of assessment, and remember that a recent benzodiazepine dose can mask it, so trend this score against the dosing chart rather than reading it alone.

exam.maneuver: Score paroxysmal sweats.
findings: 4 - Beads of sweat obvious on forehead
exam.how: Observation.
exam.meaning: Sweating comes in bursts (paroxysms) as the autonomic nervous system surges, which is why the item is scored on what is visible during the assessment rather than on the patient's report. Drenching sweats with a rising total score warn that withdrawal is escalating toward delirium tremens. Score only sweating that the room temperature and fever do not explain; if the patient is septic or febrile for another reason, say so in the note.

exam.maneuver: Score anxiety.
findings: 4 - Moderately anxious, or guarded, so anxiety is inferred
7 - Equivalent to acute panic states, as seen in severe delirium or acute schizophrenic psychoses
exam.how: Ask: "Do you feel nervous?" Observation.
exam.meaning: Anxiety in withdrawal is driven by the same excitatory rebound as the tremor, and it usually rises and falls with the total score. The 4 anchor covers the guarded patient who denies anxiety but shows it, which is common in patients minimizing their drinking. A 7 is not ordinary nervousness; it is the terror of delirium. New severe anxiety out of proportion to the rest of the score should also prompt a search for hypoglycemia, thyrotoxicosis, or sepsis.

exam.maneuver: Score agitation.
findings: 7 - Paces back and forth during most of the interview, or constantly thrashes about
exam.how: Observation.
exam.meaning: Agitation is the item that most directly drives safety decisions. A patient pacing or thrashing needs medication now, a sitter, and a room check for lines and tubes that can be pulled. Rising agitation despite adequate benzodiazepine dosing is a delirium tremens warning and a reason to escalate care rather than simply repeat the same dose.

exam.maneuver: Score tactile disturbances.
findings: 1 - Very mild itching, pins and needles, burning, or numbness
2 - Mild itching, pins and needles, burning, or numbness
3 - Moderate itching, pins and needles, burning, or numbness
exam.how: Ask: "Have you had any itching, pins and needles sensations, burning, numbness, or do you feel bugs crawling on or under your skin?" Observation.
exam.meaning: This item grades a progression from simple paresthesias to formication (the feeling of bugs crawling on or under the skin) to frank tactile hallucinations. Scores of 4 and above mean hallucinations are present, which moves the patient out of uncomplicated withdrawal and toward alcoholic hallucinosis or delirium tremens. Always ask the question as written; patients rarely volunteer these symptoms.

exam.maneuver: Score auditory disturbances.
findings: 1 - Very mild harshness or ability to frighten
2 - Mild harshness or ability to frighten
3 - Moderate harshness or ability to frighten
exam.how: Ask: "Are you more aware of sounds around you? Are they harsh? Do they frighten you? Do you hear anything disturbing? Do you hear things you know are not there?" Observation.
exam.meaning: Early auditory disturbance in withdrawal is hyperacusis: ordinary sounds feel harsh and startling. Only the upper half of the scale is hallucination. Auditory hallucinations with a clear sensorium and normal orientation suggest alcoholic hallucinosis, while the same hallucinations with disorientation point to delirium tremens, which is why this item is always read together with the orientation item.

exam.maneuver: Score visual disturbances.
exam.how: Ask: "Does the light appear to be too bright? Is its color different? Does it hurt your eyes? Are you seeing anything that is disturbing to you? Are you seeing things you know are not there?" Observation.
exam.meaning: Photophobia is the early form of this item; visual hallucinations in withdrawal are typically animals, insects, or figures in the periphery. New visual hallucinations in a withdrawing patient are delirium tremens until proven otherwise, especially with fever, tachycardia, and disorientation. Score what the patient reports even if the room looks normal to you, and document the content in the detail field.

exam.maneuver: Score headache, fullness in head.
exam.how: Ask: "Does your head feel different? Do you feel pressure?" Do not rate for dizziness or lightheadedness. Otherwise, rate severity.
exam.meaning: Headache is the only CIWA-Ar item scored purely on the patient's rating of severity, with no observational anchors. It is also the least specific item: dehydration, caffeine withdrawal, and a hangover all score here. A sudden worst-ever headache or a headache with focal findings is not withdrawal and needs its own workup rather than points on this scale.

exam.maneuver: Score orientation and clouding of sensorium.
findings: 0 - Oriented and can perform serial additions
1 - Cannot perform serial additions or is uncertain about the date
2 - Disoriented for date by no more than 2 calendar days
3 - Disoriented for date by more than 2 calendar days
exam.how: Ask: "What day is this? Where are you? Who am I?" Serial additions (the original scale's serial-addition task; many protocols use serial 7s or counting forward by threes).
exam.meaning: This is the only item scored 0 to 4, and it carries the most prognostic weight per point. Disorientation is what separates delirium tremens from uncomplicated withdrawal: hallucinations with full orientation are alcoholic hallucinosis, while hallucinations with disorientation and autonomic instability are delirium tremens, which still carries real mortality untreated. Any score above 0 in a patient whose other items are improving should trigger a search for another cause of delirium, including infection, hypoglycemia, and Wernicke encephalopathy.

exam.maneuver: Add the 10 item scores and place the total in a band (maximum 67).
findings: Less than 8 - Minimal to mild withdrawal: supportive care and repeat scoring, usually no scheduled benzodiazepine
8 to 15 - Moderate withdrawal (marked autonomic arousal): symptom-triggered benzodiazepine per protocol
15 or more - Severe withdrawal: aggressive symptom-triggered dosing, close monitoring, consider a higher level of care
exam.how: Sum exam-01 through exam-10 and re-score on the schedule your unit's protocol sets (commonly every 4 hours, and 1 hour after a dose in moderate to severe withdrawal).
exam.meaning: These bands follow the ASAM Patient Placement Criteria guideline text. A second widely used labeling (UpToDate pocket card) calls less than 10 very mild, 10 to 15 mild, 16 to 20 modest, and greater than 20 severe, so the same total can carry a different label in different documents; the number, not the label, is what the next clinician acts on, so always chart the number. Scores above 15 predict a higher risk of seizures and delirium tremens. Two cautions: a score can be low in a patient who cannot report symptoms (intubated, aphasic, severely demented), where the scale under-reads and objective scales are preferred; and thiamine, fluids, and potassium, magnesium, and phosphate repletion are part of withdrawal care at every band, not an afterthought at the severe end.

exam.maneuver: Score resting pulse rate.
exam.how: Measured after the patient has been sitting or lying for one minute. Record the actual beats per minute in the detail field.
exam.meaning: Pulse is the scale's anchor vital sign. Loss of opioid effect releases sympathetic tone, so the resting heart rate climbs as withdrawal deepens. Only score elevation that withdrawal explains: pain, fever, anxiety, recent exertion, and stimulant use all raise the pulse and, by the scale's own instruction, do not count.

exam.maneuver: Score sweating.
findings: 0 - No report of chills or flushing
1 - Subjective report of chills or flushing
2 - Flushed or observable moistness on face
3 - Beads of sweat on brow or face
exam.how: Over the past half hour, not accounted for by room temperature or patient activity.
exam.meaning: Patients often describe this as feeling hot and cold at the same time. The item is graded from report (1) to directly observable sweating (2 and above), and that observed end is part of what makes the COWS useful before buprenorphine induction, where objective signs carry more weight than symptoms the patient may be amplifying or minimizing.

exam.maneuver: Score restlessness.
findings: 1 - Reports difficulty sitting still, but is able to do so
3 - Frequent shifting or extraneous movements of legs or arms
5 - Unable to sit still for more than a few seconds
exam.how: Observation during the assessment.
exam.meaning: Restlessness is scored from watching the patient through the whole interview, not from a single glance. A patient who scores 5 here cannot hold still long enough for a reliable conversation about treatment, which is itself clinically useful information. Distinguish it from akathisia and from anxiety-driven fidgeting in a patient who is not withdrawing.

exam.maneuver: Score pupil size.
findings: 0 - Pupils pinned or normal size for room light
1 - Pupils possibly larger than normal for room light
5 - Pupils so dilated that only the rim of the iris is visible
exam.how: Judge pupil size against the room light, and check before shining a bright light for the pupillary reflex.
exam.meaning: Pupil size is the most objective item on the scale. Opioids constrict pupils; withdrawal dilates them, and dilation cannot be produced voluntarily, which is why induction protocols lean on it. The jump from 2 to 5 is in the original scale: a 5 means the iris is almost entirely gone. Recent use of other drugs (stimulants dilate, and a just-used opioid dose constricts) can override the withdrawal signal, so read this item with the use timeline.

exam.maneuver: Score bone or joint aches.
findings: 2 - Patient reports severe diffuse aching of joints or muscles
4 - Patient is rubbing joints or muscles and is unable to sit still because of discomfort
exam.how: If the patient was having pain previously, only the additional component attributed to opiate withdrawal is scored.
exam.meaning: The deep, diffuse ache is the symptom behind the phrase kicking the habit and much of the misery patients describe. The scoring caveat matters on a real service: many patients have chronic pain that predates withdrawal, and scoring all of it as withdrawal inflates the total. Score only the increment the withdrawal added.

exam.maneuver: Score runny nose or tearing.
findings: 1 - Nasal stuffiness or unusually moist eyes
4 - Nose constantly running or tears streaming down cheeks
exam.how: Not accounted for by cold symptoms or allergies.
exam.meaning: Rhinorrhea and lacrimation are parasympathetic rebound signs and part of why opioid withdrawal looks like a bad flu. They are also observable, which again helps when a score will gate a medication decision. Ask about allergies and a concurrent cold before scoring, per the scale's instruction.

exam.maneuver: Score GI upset.
findings: 5 - Multiple episodes of diarrhea or vomiting
exam.how: Over the last half hour.
exam.meaning: Opioids slow the gut; withdrawal speeds it up, and cramps typically arrive before vomiting and diarrhea. A score of 5 means the patient is losing fluid and may need volume and electrolyte replacement alongside withdrawal treatment. Chart the actual episodes in the detail field, because the count is what the next team member needs.

exam.maneuver: Score tremor.
findings: 1 - Tremor can be felt, but not observed
exam.how: Observation of outstretched hands.
exam.meaning: Tremor here is scored the same way as on the alcohol scale: feel first, then look. Muscle twitching at 4 is a late, gross sign. In a patient withdrawing from both opioids and alcohol or benzodiazepines, tremor belongs to both syndromes and the sedative withdrawal is the dangerous one; a high tremor score is a reason to run the CIWA-Ar as well, not instead.

exam.maneuver: Score yawning.
findings: 1 - Yawning once or twice during assessment
2 - Yawning three or more times during assessment
exam.how: Observation during the assessment.
exam.meaning: Yawning is an early and oddly specific withdrawal sign that often appears before the autonomic symptoms peak. It costs nothing to count: keep a rough tally during the interview so this item is scored from observation rather than estimated afterward.

exam.maneuver: Score anxiety or irritability.
findings: 1 - Patient reports increasing irritability or anxiousness
4 - Patient is so irritable or anxious that participation in the assessment is difficult
exam.how: Observation and patient report during the assessment.
exam.meaning: Irritability is frequently the symptom that brings the interaction to a head, and a 4 tells the team the interview itself is failing, which is data, not a character judgment. Score the behavior you see; a patient who is anxious because of bad news, pain, or nicotine withdrawal is showing something real, but by the scale's instruction only the opioid-withdrawal component counts.

exam.maneuver: Score gooseflesh skin.
findings: 3 - Piloerection of skin can be felt or hairs standing up on arms
exam.how: Feel the skin of the arms; look for hairs standing up. The original scale has no 1, 2, or 4 level for this item.
exam.meaning: Gooseflesh is the source of the phrase cold turkey: the skin of a withdrawing patient resembles a plucked turkey. Like pupil size, piloerection is involuntary and hard to fake, so a 3 or 5 here is strong objective evidence that withdrawal is genuinely underway, exactly the evidence wanted before a first dose of buprenorphine.

exam.maneuver: Add the 11 item scores and place the total in a band, then apply the induction rule below.
exam.how: Sum exam-01 through exam-11. The published form prints no band below 5; a total of 4 or less is below the mild band. Repeat the COWS serially during induction, as the published form's timed columns anticipate (before the first dose, then at set intervals after it).
exam.meaning: Why the total gates buprenorphine: buprenorphine binds the mu-opioid receptor very tightly but activates it only partially. Given to a patient whose receptors are still occupied by a full agonist such as heroin, fentanyl, or methadone, it pushes the full agonist off and replaces strong activation with partial activation, which the body experiences as sudden, severe withdrawal, called precipitated withdrawal. Waiting until the COWS shows withdrawal already underway means most receptors have emptied on their own, so the same dose relieves symptoms instead. SAMHSA TIP 63 frames the threshold as mild to moderate withdrawal; published protocols operationalize it anywhere from a COWS above 8 to 12 or more before the first dose, with longer waits after long-acting opioids such as methadone. For methadone-maintained patients this worksheet is only part of the picture, because methadone withdrawal itself is scored with the same scale but induction timing is far more conservative. Score honestly: an inflated COWS to justify an early dose produces exactly the precipitated withdrawal the gate exists to prevent.

history.question: When was your last drink, and how much have you been drinking on a typical day?
listenFor: Last drink within the past 12 hours
Last drink more than 48 hours ago
Still drinking daily, has not stopped yet
history.meaning: Withdrawal runs on a clock that starts at the last drink. Early symptoms (tremor, sweating, nausea, anxiety, racing pulse) begin 6 to 24 hours after the last drink. Withdrawal seizures cluster at 6 to 48 hours, and delirium tremens usually arrives at 48 to 96 hours. Knowing the last drink tells you which window the patient is in now and which dangers are still ahead, and a patient who stopped 3 days ago and feels fine is in a different position from one who stopped this morning. Amount and duration matter too: heavier, longer drinking means a deeper physical dependence and a higher chance of a severe course.

history.question: Have you ever had a seizure, delirium tremens, or hallucinations when you stopped drinking before, or needed hospital detox?
listenFor: Never had seizures, delirium, or hallucinations in withdrawal
Prior delirium tremens or ICU detox
Multiple prior detoxes, each one worse (kindling)
history.meaning: A past complicated withdrawal is the single strongest predictor of the next one. Withdrawal also shows kindling: each episode tends to be worse than the one before, because repeated cycles of excess excitation leave the brain easier to excite. A patient with a prior withdrawal seizure or delirium tremens should not be managed with watchful waiting; per the ASAM guideline they are high risk for severe or complicated withdrawal and should get early, assertive benzodiazepine treatment (front-loading) and a monitored setting.

history.question: In the last few months, have you had blackouts, used benzodiazepines or other sedatives or drugs, or been intoxicated in the last month?
listenFor: Blackouts or intoxication in the past 30 days
Benzodiazepine, barbiturate, or other drug use in the past 90 days
history.meaning: These questions come from the Prediction of Alcohol Withdrawal Severity Scale (PAWSS), a 10-item checklist for medically ill inpatients that also asks about prior withdrawal, prior detox, a positive blood alcohol level, and signs of autonomic overactivity (fast pulse, sweating, nausea). A PAWSS score of 4 or more flagged severe withdrawal with about 93% sensitivity and over 99% specificity in its validation study, though it has not been independently validated since. Concurrent sedative use matters separately: a brain tolerant to benzodiazepines as well as alcohol often needs much larger doses to settle.

history.question: Do you have liver disease, a seizure disorder from any other cause, lung disease, or other major medical problems?
listenFor: Seizure disorder, head injury, or other brain disease
Serious heart, lung, or kidney disease, or active infection
history.meaning: Comorbidity changes both the risk and the drug choice. Liver disease is the big one: the long-acting benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam) are broken down by oxidation in the liver and have active breakdown products that pile up when the liver fails, while lorazepam and oxazepam are cleared by conjugation (glucuronidation), a pathway that keeps working longer in liver disease, and have no active metabolites. Older patients and patients with lung disease are also more sensitive to sedation and respiratory depression, which argues for the shorter, cleaner agents.

history.question: Since you stopped or cut down, have you had shaking, sweating, nausea, vomiting, anxiety, or trouble sleeping?
listenFor: Mild tremor, sweating, nausea, poor sleep
Vomiting, marked tremor, racing pulse, severe anxiety
Seeing or hearing things, confusion, or a seizure already
history.meaning: The symptom pattern places the patient on the severity ladder. Tremor, sweating, nausea, insomnia, and a fast pulse are autonomic overactivity, the engine of early withdrawal. Hallucinations with a clear mind (the patient knows the images are not real and is otherwise oriented) are withdrawal hallucinosis, typically 12 to 48 hours in. Hallucinations plus confusion and disorientation are delirium, a different and far more dangerous problem. A seizure that has already happened reclassifies the whole episode as complicated withdrawal no matter how well the patient looks now.

exam.maneuver: Score withdrawal severity with the CIWA-Ar and grade it.
findings: Seizure, hallucinations, or confusion at any score: complicated
exam.how: Score the 10 CIWA-Ar items (nausea, tremor, sweats, anxiety, agitation, tactile, auditory and visual disturbances, headache, orientation), each 0 to 7 except orientation 0 to 4, and add them. Reassess on a schedule, often every 1 to 4 hours while symptoms are active. Per the ASAM guideline, CIWA-Ar was built to monitor withdrawal that is already being treated, not to make the diagnosis, and it needs a patient who can answer questions; it cannot be scored reliably in a delirious or intubated patient.
exam.meaning: The score drives dosing in symptom-triggered protocols and tracks whether treatment is winning. ASAM 2020 grades withdrawal as mild under 10, moderate 10 to 18, and severe at 19 or higher, and calls withdrawal complicated when there is a seizure, delirium, or hallucinations regardless of score. Note that many hospital protocols use different cutoffs (often 8 to 15 as moderate and over 15 as severe), so follow local protocol numbers when they differ. A rising score despite treatment is itself an escalation signal.

exam.maneuver: Choose a dosing strategy: symptom-triggered, fixed schedule, or front-loading.
findings: Mild symptoms, low risk, staff can score reliably: symptom-triggered dosing
Cannot report symptoms, unreliable scoring, or needs guaranteed coverage: fixed schedule with extra as-needed doses
High CIWA-Ar score or high risk of severe withdrawal: front-load a long-acting benzodiazepine early
exam.meaning: Benzodiazepines are first-line treatment because they reduce withdrawal seizures and delirium, the two complications that kill. In symptom-triggered dosing, medication is given only when the CIWA-Ar crosses a threshold (for example 8 to 10), in an amount tied to the score; trials show this shortens treatment and lowers the total dose compared with fixed schedules. Fixed schedules give set doses at set times with a taper, plus extra doses if needed, and fit patients who cannot be scored. Front-loading gives repeated moderate to high doses of a long-acting agent early to get control fast in severe or high-risk withdrawal; the long half-life then provides a built-in taper.

exam.maneuver: Pick the benzodiazepine based on the liver, age, and route available.
findings: Healthy liver: chlordiazepoxide or diazepam (long-acting, smooth self-taper)
Liver disease, older age, or significant lung disease: lorazepam or oxazepam
Vomiting, severe agitation, or no oral access: lorazepam IV or IM
exam.meaning: No benzodiazepine has proven more effective than the others overall; the choice is about drug handling. Chlordiazepoxide and diazepam last a long time and taper themselves, which smooths symptoms and guards against seizures, but both depend on liver oxidation and have active metabolites that accumulate in liver disease and in older patients. Lorazepam and oxazepam are cleared by conjugation, have no active metabolites, and are the safer default when the liver is sick; lorazepam also has reliable absorption by vein or muscle, unlike chlordiazepoxide and diazepam given IM. Phenobarbital is an accepted alternative or add-on in severe withdrawal in monitored settings per ASAM, especially when benzodiazepines are not controlling symptoms.

exam.maneuver: Give thiamine before any glucose, and look hard for Wernicke encephalopathy.
findings: No Wernicke signs: prophylactic thiamine given before dextrose
Confusion, unsteady gait, or abnormal eye movements: treat as Wernicke now
Dextrose already running and thiamine not given: give thiamine immediately
exam.how: For prevention in a patient who can absorb oral medication, 100 mg thiamine daily is the common protocol dose; use the IV route when the patient is vomiting, malnourished, or high risk. For suspected Wernicke encephalopathy, most reviews and the European Federation of Neurological Societies guideline use 500 mg IV three times daily for at least 2 to 3 days, then reassess; doses in the literature vary widely and the old FDA label regimen (100 mg IV then 50 to 100 mg IM daily) is widely considered too low. Also replace potassium, magnesium, and phosphate, give folate and a multivitamin, and rehydrate.
exam.meaning: Glucose consumes thiamine. In a thiamine-starved brain, a dose of dextrose without thiamine can tip the patient into Wernicke encephalopathy, so the order is always thiamine first, glucose second. The classic Wernicke triad is confusion, gait ataxia, and eye findings (nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia), but most patients do not show all three, and waiting for the full triad misses cases; any one feature in a heavy drinker is enough to treat. Untreated Wernicke can progress to Korsakoff syndrome, a permanent amnesia, while thiamine is cheap and low-risk, so the threshold to treat should be very low.

exam.maneuver: Recognize withdrawal that is outrunning treatment and escalate the level of care.
findings: Symptoms persist despite large benzodiazepine doses: resistant withdrawal
Delirium, fever, or unstable pulse and blood pressure: ICU-level care
Withdrawal seizure: benzodiazepine now, then load and monitor closely
exam.meaning: ASAM uses the term resistant alcohol withdrawal for severe symptoms that persist despite high-dose benzodiazepines; there is no agreed dose that defines it, though studies have used cutoffs such as 200 mg of diazepam within 4 hours. Resistant withdrawal, delirium tremens, and autonomic instability (fever, wild swings in pulse and blood pressure) need a higher level of care, continuous monitoring, and usually added agents such as phenobarbital or, in intubated patients, propofol, managed with critical care. Also look for the problems that travel with withdrawal and worsen it: infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, pancreatitis, and low potassium, magnesium, and phosphate. Deaths in withdrawal usually come from delirium, hyperthermia, arrhythmia, or a missed second diagnosis, not from tremor.

exam.maneuver: Set the monitoring plan and the treatment goal for the next 24 hours.
findings: Mild and low risk: monitor for up to 36 hours for worsening
Moderate to severe: scheduled CIWA-Ar checks with vital signs until clearly improving
Improving and past the seizure window: taper, start relapse-prevention medication, arrange follow-up
exam.meaning: Withdrawal care is a trajectory, not a single dose. ASAM suggests monitoring even low-risk patients with mild withdrawal for up to 36 hours because symptoms can climb. The danger windows are front-loaded: seizures mostly in the first 48 hours, delirium tremens at 48 to 96 hours, occasionally later. Once a patient is clearly improving and past the seizure window, the job changes from rescue to relapse prevention: offer a medication for alcohol use disorder (naltrexone, acamprosate, or disulfiram) and a concrete follow-up plan before discharge, because detox alone without follow-on treatment rarely changes the course of the disease.

history.question: What opioids have you been using, how much each day, and when did you last use?
listenFor: Short-acting opioids (heroin, oxycodone, hydrocodone), last use within the past day
Methadone or buprenorphine, prescribed or not
Last use more than 72 hours ago
history.meaning: The drug, the dose, and the clock decide when induction is safe. Buprenorphine can only be started once enough of the full agonist has left the receptors, and long-acting drugs leave slowly: methadone lingers for days, and fentanyl, although it feels short-acting, is stored in fat and leaches back out, so people who use fentanyl can precipitate withdrawal even after a day or more of abstinence. A clear last-use history also tells you how much tolerance you are treating, which separates a patient who will settle on standard doses from one who needs a methadone program.

history.question: Have you ever taken buprenorphine, methadone, or naltrexone before? What happened?
listenFor: Never tried any medication for opioid use disorder
Did well on one of them before
Sudden severe withdrawal right after a first dose (precipitated withdrawal)
Stopped because of side effects, cost, or clinic rules
history.meaning: Past response is the best guide to the next prescription. A patient who did well on methadone years ago will often do well again, and a patient who had precipitated withdrawal after buprenorphine needs a different induction plan (more objective withdrawal first, a low-dose induction, or methadone instead), not just reassurance. Ask exactly what happened: feeling much worse within an hour or two of the first buprenorphine dose is precipitated withdrawal; feeling no effect, or disliking daily clinic visits, is a different problem with a different fix.

history.question: Are you pregnant, or is there a chance you could be pregnant?
listenFor: Unsure: needs a pregnancy test before choosing a medication
history.meaning: Pregnancy changes the counseling, not the commitment to treat. Methadone and buprenorphine are the standard of care in pregnancy, and medically supervised withdrawal is generally avoided because relapse rates are high and relapse exposes the fetus to cycles of intoxication and withdrawal plus all the risks of the drug supply. Naltrexone has limited safety data in pregnancy, so starting it is a specialist decision rather than a default. Test when the answer is unsure, because the result changes which conversations you need to have today.

history.question: If you used and overdosed, would anyone be there? Do you have naloxone at home?
listenFor: Someone nearby, but no naloxone in the home
Naloxone in the home and a household member knows how to use it
history.meaning: Most fatal overdoses happen when the person is alone with no one to give naloxone or call for help. Asking this question identifies the patients who most need a naloxone kit in hand, a household member taught to use it, and counseling about not using alone. Tolerance also falls fast during abstinence, detox, incarceration, and the first weeks on an antagonist, so a dose that was routine a month ago can kill now; that warning belongs in every discharge conversation.

exam.maneuver: Score the Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) before the first buprenorphine dose, and look for objective signs.
findings: COWS under 5: no real withdrawal yet, wait
COWS 13 to 24: moderate withdrawal, the usual induction window
COWS 25 or higher: moderately severe to severe withdrawal
exam.how: COWS rates 11 items: resting pulse, sweating, restlessness, pupil size, bone and joint aches, runny nose or tearing, GI upset, tremor, yawning, anxiety or irritability, and gooseflesh. Bands: 5 to 12 mild, 13 to 24 moderate, 25 to 36 moderately severe, over 36 severe. Trust the objective items (pupil size, gooseflesh, GI upset, tremor) over the reported ones when deciding to dose.
exam.meaning: Buprenorphine grips the mu opioid receptor more tightly than heroin, fentanyl, or oxycodone but activates it only partly. If it is given while a full agonist still occupies the receptors, it knocks the stronger drug off and replaces a full signal with a partial one, and the patient crashes into sudden, severe withdrawal within an hour or two: precipitated withdrawal. Waiting for objective withdrawal means most receptors are already empty, so the partial signal is a relief instead of a loss. Protocols set the floor differently (some say a COWS of 8, many say 12 to 13), and with fentanyl, precipitation can still occur at higher scores, which is why visible signs matter more than any single number.

exam.maneuver: Give the first buprenorphine dose and reassess before deciding the day 1 total.
findings: Withdrawal clearly better 1 to 2 hours after the dose: continue titrating
Withdrawal much worse soon after the dose: precipitated withdrawal
Still in moderate withdrawal and tolerating doses: add more buprenorphine
exam.meaning: Standard induction starts with 2 to 4 mg under the tongue once objective withdrawal is present, reassesses in 1 to 2 hours, and adds doses as needed; day 1 totals commonly reach 16 mg, with most patients stabilizing at 12 to 16 mg daily (SAMHSA TIP 63 practice). If precipitated withdrawal happens, the counterintuitive but correct move is more buprenorphine, which fills the remaining receptors with the partial agonist and usually settles symptoms over hours, plus symptom medications such as clonidine for autonomic symptoms. For patients who cannot tolerate waiting for withdrawal, especially with fentanyl or methadone, low-dose induction overlaps tiny, slowly rising buprenorphine doses with the full agonist over about a week; published schedules vary, so use a local protocol. The naloxone in combination products is there to deter injection and is barely absorbed under the tongue; it does not cause the withdrawal, the buprenorphine does.

exam.maneuver: Decide whether methadone fits this patient better than buprenorphine.
findings: Very high tolerance, or buprenorphine has failed or precipitated repeatedly: methadone through an opioid treatment program
Needs the structure of daily observed dosing and an intensive program
Long QT, many interacting medicines, or erratic attendance: methadone risk is higher, weigh carefully
exam.meaning: Methadone is a full mu agonist with no ceiling, so it can match any level of tolerance, which is why it retains patients with the heaviest use; the price is that respiratory depression never plateaus, and because the drug accumulates over the first several days, the most dangerous days are often days 3 to 5, when the patient looks settled but the level is still climbing. It also prolongs the QT interval and interacts with many medicines. For opioid use disorder it may only be dispensed by a certified opioid treatment program (OTP); a hospital can give it to a patient admitted for something else, but cannot hand out a prescription for addiction treatment. Under SAMHSA's 2024 rule, the first dose may now be up to 50 mg (raised from 30 mg), and take-home doses are far more flexible than the old schedule: up to 7 unsupervised doses in the first 14 days, up to 14 in days 15 to 30, and up to 28 after day 31, based on practitioner judgment.

exam.maneuver: Check that the patient is fully opioid-free before any naltrexone, and pick oral versus monthly injection.
findings: Opioid-free 7 to 10 days, motivated, wants an antagonist: candidate
Used opioids within the past week, or coming off methadone or buprenorphine within 2 weeks: do not start
Daily pills unrealistic: monthly extended-release injection instead
exam.meaning: Naltrexone is a pure opioid antagonist: it treats nothing today and blocks opioids for as long as it is on board. Given too early it precipitates withdrawal just as surely as buprenorphine given too early, so the label requires at least 7 to 10 days opioid-free, and up to 2 weeks for patients coming off methadone or buprenorphine; a urine screen and, when in doubt, a naloxone challenge come first. Oral naltrexone is 50 mg daily and fails mainly through missed doses. Extended-release naltrexone is 380 mg injected monthly and suits patients who have completed detox and can plan around it, a group where it has its strongest track record. Warn every patient that tolerance is gone: trying to override the blockade, or using again after the injection wears off, carries a real overdose risk.

exam.maneuver: Adjust the medication plan for pregnancy.
findings: Pregnant: methadone or buprenorphine is the standard of care
Medically supervised withdrawal in pregnancy: not recommended as the plan
Naltrexone in pregnancy: limited data, specialist decision, not a default start
exam.meaning: Untreated opioid use disorder in pregnancy means repeated cycles of intoxication and withdrawal for the fetus, plus the infection, trauma, and overdose risks of the drug supply; agonist treatment steadies all of that, which is why ACOG and ASAM endorse methadone or buprenorphine rather than detox. Buprenorphine without naloxone was the traditional product in pregnancy, though the combination product is now widely used and accepted. Expect neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome in a substantial share of exposed newborns; it is anticipated, monitored for, and treatable, and it is not by itself a reason to avoid agonist therapy or to report a mother who is engaged in treatment.

exam.maneuver: Confirm what you may prescribe, dispense, or only administer, in 2026 rules.
findings: Buprenorphine: any DEA registration with Schedule III authority, no waiver, no patient cap
Methadone for opioid use disorder: only through a certified opioid treatment program
Hospital or ED, patient in withdrawal, no program bed yet: you may administer opioids for up to 72 hours while arranging treatment
exam.meaning: The X-waiver is gone. Section 1262 of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 (the MAT Act) removed the federal waiver and patient caps for buprenorphine, so any clinician whose DEA registration includes Schedule III authority can prescribe it where state law allows; the remaining federal training item is the MATE Act's one-time 8-hour substance use disorder training attestation tied to DEA registration or renewal. Methadone is the exception: for addiction treatment it still runs only through certified OTPs. The bridge rule is 21 CFR 1306.07(b): a practitioner who is not an OTP may administer, but not prescribe, opioids to relieve acute withdrawal symptoms for up to 3 days, one day at a time, while arranging referral. That rule is what lets an ED or hospital team keep a patient comfortable and engaged instead of losing them to withdrawal-driven departure.

exam.maneuver: Close every MOUD start with naloxone, a tolerance warning, and a near-term follow-up.
findings: Naloxone kit in hand and a household member shown how to use it
Follow-up appointment within days, with a named clinic or prescriber
Patient can state that their tolerance is lower now than it was
exam.meaning: Starting medication is a beginning, not a discharge summary. Co-prescribing naloxone with MOUD is recommended practice, and the kit only helps if someone besides the patient knows where it is and how to use it, since the patient cannot reverse their own overdose. The highest-risk moments are transitions: the first weeks of treatment, any gap in doses, release from jail or hospital, and the weeks after an antagonist injection wears off. A follow-up measured in days, with a warm handoff to a named prescriber or program, is what turns an induction into treatment.

sheets.title: Intoxication, withdrawal, and urine drug testing

history.question: What did you take, how much, how did you take it, and when?
listenFor: Several substances, or pills or powder from the street
Unknown substance, found down or brought in by others
history.meaning: The history sets the differential, but in street-drug presentations it is often incomplete or wrong: fentanyl is sold as heroin and pressed into counterfeit pills, and xylazine and other adulterants ride along. Treat the reported history as a starting hypothesis and let the exam pattern (the toxidrome) confirm or replace it. Route and timing matter for what comes next: smoked and injected drugs peak in minutes, swallowed pills may not peak for hours, and a patient who looks well 30 minutes after swallowing a handful of tablets has not yet declared themselves.

history.question: What medicines do you take regularly, including over-the-counter medicines, supplements, and anything borrowed from someone else?
listenFor: Bupropion, tramadol, diphenhydramine, dextromethorphan, or other false-positive sources
Serotonin-active medicines: antidepressants, linezolid, triptans, St John's wort
history.meaning: The medication list explains half of all confusing drug screens and many confusing exams. Bupropion, pseudoephedrine, labetalol, and trazodone can trip the amphetamine assay; dextromethorphan, diphenhydramine, tramadol, and venlafaxine can trip the PCP assay; poppy seeds, rifampin, and fluoroquinolone antibiotics can trip the opiate assay. Prescribed benzodiazepines such as lorazepam and clonazepam commonly fail to appear on the benzodiazepine assay, which is built to detect other family members. Serotonin-active combinations set up serotonin toxicity, which mimics stimulant intoxication but is treated differently (benzodiazepines, cooling, and cyproheptadine rather than more sedation alone).

history.question: When did you last use each substance, and how often have you been using?
listenFor: More than a week ago, or daily heavy use for months
history.meaning: Last-use timing is what makes a urine result interpretable. Most stimulants, cocaine, and short-acting opioids clear urine in 1 to 4 days, so a negative screen on day 5 does not contradict a truthful history of use last week, and a positive THC screen can reflect use from weeks ago in a daily user rather than use today. Frequency matters as much as timing: fat-soluble drugs (THC, fentanyl, PCP, long-acting benzodiazepines) accumulate with daily use and stay detectable far longer than after a single exposure. Always pair the result with the question, 'when did you last use,' before concluding anything.

exam.maneuver: Look for the opioid intoxication pattern.
findings: Slow or shallow breathing, pinpoint pupils, decreased consciousness: opioid triad
Pinpoint pupils and sedation but breathing adequate: opioid effect, monitor
Track marks, skin abscesses, or a naloxone response that confirms the pattern
exam.how: Check the respiratory rate and depth first, then pupils, bowel sounds (quiet in opioid effect), and level of consciousness. A trial of naloxone that restores breathing is both treatment and strong diagnostic evidence.
exam.meaning: The opioid toxidrome is respiratory depression, miosis (pinpoint pupils), and depressed consciousness, with quiet bowel sounds and cool skin. What kills is the breathing, so the pattern matters more than the pupil size, which can be normal with some opioids or when other drugs are mixed in. Fentanyl can also cause chest wall rigidity when given or taken rapidly in large amounts. Because naloxone wears off in 30 to 90 minutes while most opioids last longer, a patient who wakes up after naloxone can slide back into respiratory depression and needs observation, not immediate discharge.

exam.maneuver: Look for opioid withdrawal, the mirror image of intoxication.
findings: Dilated pupils, tearing, runny nose, yawning, gooseflesh
Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, loud bowel sounds, muscle aches
Anxious and uncomfortable but alert, with normal or mildly fast vital signs
exam.meaning: Opioid withdrawal flips every sign: pupils dilate, secretions pour (tearing, rhinorrhea, sweating), the gut speeds up (cramping, vomiting, diarrhea, hyperactive bowel sounds), and piloerection gives 'cold turkey' its name. In a healthy adult it is miserable rather than dangerous, unlike alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, which can kill. The real dangers are dehydration in frail patients, suicide risk in despairing ones, and patients leaving against medical advice before other treatment finishes; untreated withdrawal is a leading, fixable cause of those departures. Score it with COWS and treat it early (see the MOUD sheet).

exam.maneuver: Look for the sympathomimetic (stimulant) pattern: cocaine, amphetamines, methamphetamine.
findings: Fast pulse and high blood pressure, fever, dilated pupils, sweating
Agitation, paranoia, or psychosis with tremor
Chest pain, seizures, or severe hyperthermia: complications in progress
exam.how: Feel the skin. In stimulant intoxication the skin is wet with sweat; in anticholinergic poisoning, which shares the fast pulse, fever, and dilated pupils, the skin is dry. That one touch separates the two.
exam.meaning: Stimulants flood the body with catecholamines: everything speeds up, pupils dilate, bowel sounds stay active, and the skin sweats. The complications are what hurt people: hyperthermia, seizures, dangerously high blood pressure, heart attack from coronary spasm or demand, and muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) from sustained agitation. Benzodiazepines are the first-line treatment because they turn down the central drive behind all of it; cooling matters when temperature climbs. Antipsychotics alone do not treat the physiology and can add risk in a hot, seizing patient.

exam.maneuver: Separate anticholinergic poisoning from stimulant intoxication.
findings: Hot, dry, flushed skin with no sweat in the armpit
Dilated pupils, delirium with mumbling and picking at invisible objects
Full bladder (urinary retention) and quiet bowel sounds
exam.meaning: The classic description is 'hot as a hare, blind as a bat, dry as a bone, red as a beet, mad as a hatter, full as a flask.' Common culprits are diphenhydramine, tricyclic antidepressants, cyclobenzaprine, scopolamine, and jimsonweed. The dry skin and quiet gut separate it from stimulant intoxication at the bedside. The delirium is a picking, mumbling, fragmented delirium rather than the organized paranoia of stimulants. Treatment is supportive care and benzodiazepines for agitation; physostigmine is a specialist (toxicology) decision, and tricyclic involvement changes the picture because of sodium channel blockade and wide-QRS arrhythmias, treated with sodium bicarbonate.
